docs.title: orfdata
docs.text: orfdata builds the protein reference for a species: the proteins annotated in a PyEnsembl genome, plus open reading frames (ORFs) that ribosome-profiling studies found translated outside those annotations. Each added ORF stays bound to its PyEnsembl transcript, with its source, category and evidence. Viral proteomes can be added explicitly, but only for a species that is a recorded host of the virus.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11 or later. Install orfdata and one PyEnsembl annotation:

python -m pip install 'orfdata'
pyensembl install --release 115 --species human
orfdata setup --species human --catalogs all  # For ncORF presets and "all"

Viral support is part of the base install; only the data is downloaded. Get the human GDC viral references — genomes, coding transcripts and proteins, as three named layers — with orfdata download viral --species human. Use orfdata download list to see every known resource and orfdata download status to see what is local. To annotate variants in viral transcripts or noncanonical ORFs with varcode, isovar, topiary or vaxrank, see Downstream tools.

The second command downloads and indexes Ensembl 115 for human GRCh38. Opening ORFdata resources never downloads them implicitly; use the explicit commands under orfdata download or the corresponding PyEnsembl command when data is missing.

docs.title: Build a human proteome
docs.text:
from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import ReferenceTranscriptome

genome = EnsemblRelease(115, species="human")
transcriptome = ReferenceTranscriptome.from_genome(genome)
reference = transcriptome.proteome()  # Reference CDS proteins only.
proteome = transcriptome.proteome(nc_orf_sources="ms")
proteome.write_fasta("human-e115.fasta")
print(proteome.summary()["kinds"], len(proteome.excluded))

{'annotated': 245535, 'extra_orf': 2181} 5

proteome() takes every reference CDS protein in the Ensembl 115 annotation. Use isoforms="longest" for one reference protein per gene, selected by length. nc_orf_sources="ms" adds the bundled human ORFs that have supporting mass-spectrometry (MS) peptides: 2,181 of the 2,186 are encoded by an Ensembl 115 transcript, which must contain the ORF's exact spliced coding path. The other 5 are listed in proteome.excluded with the reason. Each entry lists every transcript encoding it. Building this human proteome takes under a minute, and proteome.save(path) keeps it as a checksummed snapshot.

The same proteome from the command line:

orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources ms --output human-e115.fasta

docs.title: Choose ncORF sources
docs.text:
nc_orf_sources= Selects ORFs with Human ORFs Encoded in Ensembl 115 "ribosome" or "riboseq" Ribosome profiling across all datasets 69,286 69,162 "ms" Any supporting MS peptide 2,186 2,181 "immunopeptidomics" Peptides eluted from MHC (in human, HLA) molecules 1,881 1,879 "proteomics" Peptides from digested cellular proteins 73 72 "all" Every compatible dataset 69,286 69,162

Use nc_orf_sources="bundled" for the bundled dataset alone, or a list of names such as ["bundled", "ncorf-mammals-human"] for a subset. Evidence presets and "all" require all compatible datasets; install human's optional datasets once with orfdata setup --species human --catalogs all. Missing resources produce installation instructions. The defaults still add no ncORFs. RibORF source catalogues include valid 1–4-residue ORFs. Apply a downstream policy explicitly with min_protein_length=5, or CLI --min-protein-length 5, when a peptide-search reference should omit them.

Most MS support in the bundled human catalogue comes from immunopeptidomics. A presented peptide shows that the ORF was translated; it does not establish a stable protein. See building a reference proteome for stricter filters and what each level means.

docs.title: Look up the ORFs on a transcript
docs.text:
Continue in the same Python session:

from orfdata import extra_orfs

orfs = extra_orfs(genome)
for orf in orfs.for_transcript(genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000304842")):  # TPST1
    print(orf.model.orf_id, orf.model.orf_type, orf.protein_sequence)
    print(orf.evidence.has_evidence("ms"))

c7riboseqorf56 uORF MPSRRRGGSSLIPDVGYLSEVDCPWPEHFPKIILSKISV
True

extra_orfs(genome) places every catalogue ORF on every transcript of this genome that carries its exact coding path; without evidence=, it includes every catalogue ORF. Each result is a TranscriptORF: the source ORF, its evidence and the original PyEnsembl transcript, with start and end slicing the transcript sequence. One RNA can have several ORFs, even when Ensembl annotates it as noncoding; the transcript's biotype and annotated protein are unchanged. Add include_annotated=True to list the annotated CDSs on that transcript alongside them.

(nc_orf_sources="all") Mouse From PyEnsembl 60,707 ORFs on GRCm39: Ribo-seq ORFs of Chang et al. and Yang et al., and 2,976 MS-supported ones (OpenProt 2.2), built locally with orfdata setup --species mouse; lifted to GRCm38 and NCBIM37 Zebrafish From PyEnsembl 15,491 GRCz11 Ribo-seq ORFs of Yang et al., built locally C. elegans From PyEnsembl 4,035 WBcel235 Ribo-seq ORFs of Yang et al., built locally Budding yeast From PyEnsembl 1,369 R64-1-1 Ribo-seq ORFs of Yang et al., built locally; 171 lie on Ensembl's transcripts Dog From PyEnsembl None: no public dog Ribo-seq or ncORF MS exists

Other assemblies use a catalogue lifted to them once orfdata chains download has fetched the chain files (with --accept-terms for UCSC's non-commercial mouse chains); see every assembly of a species. with_nc_orfs() raises for a species without a catalogue, or whose catalogue or chains aren't installed yet, rather than returning an annotated-only proteome. Human ORF evidence is never transferred to another species. The same API also serves RNA, ribosome and protein measurements for human, mouse, dog and yeast; see released data and gaps.

docs.title: Optional ORF catalogues
docs.text:
The bundled human catalogue is available through load_catalog() without downloads. CatalogRegistry manages additional versioned ORF catalogues, with the same explicit discovery, download, build and offline-open workflow as DatasetRegistry. Once a species' catalogue in the packaged registry is downloaded or built, load_catalog(species=...) opens it, so extra_orfs(genome) and Proteome.with_nc_orfs("all") use registered sources. Pass load_catalog(species=..., registry=...) as nc_orf_sources= to a proteome constructor for your own registry. Every catalogue for the species is used, merged: those on the requested assembly as they are, and those on another assembly the pinned chains reach, lifted (details). Each catalogue contributes its release on the requested assembly if it has one, else its default release. It returns the existing ORFCatalog; query results still bind to the original PyEnsembl transcript through ReferenceORF. To use several catalogues for one species together, see merging catalogues.

The packaged registry supplies catalogues as pinned downloads or builds from their sources' own files:

Species Catalogues ORFs Mouse OpenProt's MS-supported ORFs, Chang et al.'s and Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs 60,707 merged Human the bundled GENCODE set; optionally Chang et al.'s and Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs 7,264; 69,286 with both Zebrafish Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs 15,491 C. elegans Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs 4,035 Yeast Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs 1,369 Dog none exists 0

orfdata setup --species mouse (or zebrafish, worm, yeast) installs a species' catalogues, with the chain files. orfdata catalogs status (in Python, catalog_status()) lists every catalogue load_catalog can open, the bundled one included, with its species, assembly, record count, whether it is installed and whether it is used:

orfdata catalogs status

The examples below use a caller-supplied registry.

import json
from orfdata import CatalogRegistry

with open("catalog-registry.json") as handle:
    registry = CatalogRegistry(json.load(handle))
releases = registry.list(species="yeast")
for manifest in releases:
    print(manifest.catalog_id, manifest.version, manifest.coverage)

# Select an entry from your populated registry.
name = releases[0].catalog_id
registry.download(name)             # Explicit, checksum-verified acquisition.
catalog = registry.open(name)       # Offline; no implicit download or repair.
records = catalog.query(evidence="ms", require_resolved=True)
orfs = catalog.for_transcript(transcript)  # An already loaded PyEnsembl transcript.

Use info(name) for immutable provenance and download_metadata(name) for artifact URLs, checksums and access terms. inspect(name) checks the local installation. Species, strain, assembly and annotation contexts remain attached to accepted records; a matching accession alone cannot transfer evidence.

orfdata catalogs --registry catalog-registry.json list --species yeast
orfdata catalogs --registry catalog-registry.json download NAME
orfdata catalogs --registry catalog-registry.json query NAME --evidence ms --require-resolved

Queries share the ordinary ORF CLI's gene, transcript, genomic-position and evidence filters, and JSON/TSV/FASTA exports. They cannot override the selected release with a local --catalog argument. Use orfdata --catalog FILE for the existing standalone local-file workflow.

docs.title: Mouse
docs.text:
pip install "orfdata"
orfdata setup --species mouse --accept-terms   # Three catalogues and the chains

orfdata setup downloads the published Chang et al. and RibORF catalogues, builds OpenProt from their pinned sources, and downloads the chain files (--accept-terms for UCSC's non-commercial GRCm38/GRCm39 chains). It prints what it did with each: built, downloaded, already installed, repaired or skipped. If one fails, the rest are still installed and it exits with status 1, naming each failure; in Python, install_species raises InstallError, whose result holds the same report. load_catalog(species="mouse") merges OpenProt, Chang et al. and Yang et al. in that order. Current inputs contain 2,976 MS-supported OpenProt ORFs, 16,484 Chang et al. ORFs and 51,831 validated Yang et al. target placements. Overlapping source models merge by coding path and protein while keeping their original evidence. Merged counts and target-genome placement counts depend on these versions; inspect the resulting catalogue and proteome layer receipts. On GRCm38 and NCBIM37 the catalogues are lifted automatically.

docs.title: Mouse Ribo-seq ORFs (Chang et al.)
docs.text:
ncorf-mammals-mouse holds the mouse ncORFs of Chang et al. (eLife 2025, doi:10.7554/eLife.109128): 16,484 of the source's 16,485, called with PRICE, RiboCode and Ribo-TISH on Ensembl 107: an ORF is kept when at least two callers find it in a library, in at least two libraries, starting at ATG, CTG, GTG or TTG. Its types are uORF (8,294), lncORF (3,576), uoORF (1,950), iORF (1,749), dORF (741) and doORF (174).

  • Download. orfdata data fetch ncorf-mammals-mouse installs the checksum-pinned 2.22 MB catalogue. orfdata data path ncorf-mammals-mouse returns its local path for offline use. Python callers use fetch_data("ncorf-mammals-mouse") and CatalogRegistry().open("ncorf-mammals-mouse"). The data release includes the manifest, source access terms and acceptance receipt. orfdata catalogs build ncorf-mammals-mouse still explicitly rebuilds from the original inputs; catalogs query ncorf-mammals-mouse --built selects that result.
  • Sources. The authors' BED and protein FASTA (MIT, pinned commit), the paper's Table S3 (CC BY 4.0) and Ensembl 107's GTF; about 40 MB.
  • Coding paths. The BED garbles multi-exon block sizes, so each ORF's path comes from its representative transcript and transcript coordinates in Ensembl 107, checked against its genomic start, stop, BED span and protein length. 16,484 resolve; one without a stop codon is listed as unresolved. All 16,484 bind to their Ensembl 107 transcript with their exact coding path and protein; 16,470 place on Ensembl 115.
  • Starts. The source writes GTG-initiated proteins with valine. A near-cognate start is read by the initiator methionine, so these proteins begin with M, and their records declare the GTG start (CTG and TTG are already starts of the standard code).
  • Evidence. Each ORF's library and caller counts become aggregate Ribo-seq summaries, so RiboSeq() selects every ORF and MS() none. The libraries aren't named per ORF, so RiboSeq(min_studies=2) selects none.

docs.title: Mouse RibORF ORFs (Yang et al.)
docs.text:
riborf-mouse generation 3 reconstructs the ORFs reported by Yang et al. (Nat Commun 2024, doi:10.1038/s41467-024-46240-9) against their original GENCODE M25/GRCm38 reference before any placement on Ensembl 107/GRCm39. The original table supplies RNA intervals and BED blocks, not protein sequences. All 54,128 non-skipped rows reconstruct against the pinned native RNA, with the full transcript version, length, start/stop and every BED block checked.

  • Download. orfdata data fetch riborf-mouse installs the verified 24.9 MB catalogue. Rebuilding remains available from its pinned source files.
  • Target placement. Exact full RNA, coding nucleotide sequence and translated protein must agree. All target cDNA and ncRNA sequences are searched, including duplicate loci and renamed transcripts. A surviving stable ID, unchanged RNA length or matching start/stop alone cannot transfer evidence.
  • Coverage. 51,831 rows have a unique validated target placement, representing 41,882 distinct proteins. Another 118 have multiple exact target placements; 2,179 lack an unchanged complete target RNA. These 2,297 retain their native models, sequences, evidence and explicit mapping reasons in catalog.metadata["unresolved"]. extra_orfs(...).unlifted also reports them under the requested evidence rule. A changed RNA with an unchanged small CDS remains unresolved under this conservative placement method.
  • Provenance. Placed records retain their native ORFRecord in record.lifted_from and a typed record.reference_mapping. The latter records source/target references, original row ID, RNA interval, native CDS, source pins, coordinate checks and exact sequence comparisons. Evidence summaries continue to name the native reference and protein. No chain file is invented; record.liftover is None. JSON and TSV exports retain both objects. Managed manifests keep target annotation contexts in references and native evidence contexts in source_references.
  • Sources. Supplementary Data 3 (CC BY 4.0), native GENCODE M25 GTF/RNA and Ensembl 107 GTF/cDNA/ncRNA: about 198 MB in total. The 32 MB target GTF is also used by Chang et al., so species setup acquires it once.
  • Evidence and length. The 224 samples in 26 GEO series provide aggregate RibORF presence, not per-ORF named studies. RiboSeq() selects the target records; MS() and RiboSeq(min_studies=2) select none. The catalogue retains 11,858 target ORFs shorter than five residues. Consumers choose length limits when querying or building proteomes.
  • IDs and earlier generations. IDs are riborf_ followed by the original source row ID, including its native transcript version and RNA interval. They do not relabel a current coordinate as an original observation. Generations 1/2 reconstructed proteins directly from the target annotation; new builds of those unvalidated generations fail before downloads and direct callers to generation 3. Archived files remain historical data, with their saved provenance; they are not retroactively sequence-validated.

The source's ouORF, odORF and noncoding categories use the common uoORF, doORF and lncORF names. Canonical CDSs, likely sequencing errors and stop-codon readthrough rows remain excluded.

docs.title: Mouse ORFs from OpenProt
docs.text:
openprot-mouse holds the alternative proteins (AltProts) and novel isoforms that OpenProt 2.2 reports for mouse with at least two unique MS peptides, on Ensembl 106 GRCm39 transcripts. orfdata does not redistribute OpenProt's files, and OpenProt states no licence for them. You build the catalogue from OpenProt's own downloads (3.4 MB, about 5 seconds), each checked against its pinned size and SHA-256, with orfdata setup --species mouse along with the Ribo-seq catalogue above, or alone with orfdata catalogs build openprot-mouse. load_catalog(species="mouse"), extra_orfs(genome) and Proteome.build(genome, nc_orf_sources="ms") use all three mouse catalogues, for any GRCm39 Ensembl release, so all must be installed. To add only MS-supported ORFs:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import Proteome

proteome = Proteome.build(EnsemblRelease(115, species="mouse"), nc_orf_sources="ms")
print(proteome.summary()["kinds"], len(proteome.excluded))

{'annotated': 66668, 'extra_orf': 2854} 122
  • Records. OpenProt's file has 8,645 rows for 2,913 proteins; each row places one protein on one transcript. The 4,074 rows on Ensembl transcripts become 2,976 records, one per protein and spliced coding path, named by the OpenProt accession (IP_ for AltProts, II_ for isoforms). The 32 proteins found at several paths, mostly identical copies at different loci such as on chrY, have one record per path (96 in all), named accession@transcript; they share one evidence summary. A path on several transcripts is one record, placed on each of them. orf_type is OpenProt's protein type.
  • Not imported. The 4,571 rows on RefSeq transcripts are listed in metadata["unresolved"], because no RefSeq annotation is pinned. Every protein still has a record: the one accession with only RefSeq rows, IP_957586, has the same sequence and path as II_957586, which is imported.
  • Genes. OpenProt gives Ensembl gene IDs, not names, so query the catalogue by gene ID (--gene ENSMUSG00000020149); proteome entries and placements take gene names from the PyEnsembl annotation. A split accession's bare ID, such as IP_824771, names all of its records.
  • Coordinates. Coding blocks come from OpenProt's BED file. Its README calls the TSV's genomic coordinates 1-based, but they are one lower than the BED's and Ensembl's at both ends (#55). The build checks every row against that offset, its transcript span and its protein length, and fails rather than guessing if any disagrees.
  • Checked on Ensembl. On Ensembl 106, OpenProt's own release, 2,864 records bind to their source transcript with their exact coding path and protein. The other 112 lie on transcripts that are in Ensembl's GTF but missing from its cDNA and ncRNA files, so there is no sequence to check. On Ensembl 115, 2,854 place; of the rest, 109 lack a sequence, 10 transcripts are gone and 3 splice paths changed. Each is listed with its reason.
  • Evidence. OpenProt's MS score (a sum of unique peptides per study) and translation-event score (a count of studies) become aggregate summaries for the protein, not peptides or named studies. So MS() selects every record and RiboSeq() the 137 placed on Ensembl 115 with translation evidence, but MS(min_peptides=2) and RiboSeq(min_studies=2) select none. A sum of per-study peptide counts is not a count of distinct peptides, and a count of studies names no studies, so neither can show two independent observations.
  • Other assemblies. GRCm38 and NCBIM37 genomes use the catalogue lifted automatically once the chains are downloaded (UCSC's GRCm39-to-GRCm38 chain needs --accept-terms); see every assembly of a species.
  • Dog. OpenProt has no dog data, and orfdata has no dog catalogue. Mouse evidence is never transferred to dog through orthology.

Cite Leblanc S, et al. OpenProt 2.0 builds a path to the functional characterization of alternative proteins. Nucleic Acids Res. 2024;52(D1):D522–D528, doi:10.1093/nar/gkad1050.

docs.title: Human Ribo-seq ORFs (optional)
docs.text:
load_catalog(species="human") defaults to the bundled GENCODE catalogue: 7,264 ORFs, offline, with no setup. Two larger Ribo-seq catalogues are optional, used only when asked for, because they would change every human selection and make loading human ORFs about 60 times slower:

orfdata setup --species human --catalogs all   # Builds both; about 225 MB of sources

from orfdata import Proteome, extra_orfs, load_catalog

catalog = load_catalog(species="human", catalogs="all")   # Bundled, Chang et al. and Yang et al., merged
orfs = extra_orfs(genome, "ribosome", catalogs="all")
proteome = Proteome.build(genome, nc_orf_sources="all")
load_catalog(species="human", catalogs=["ncorf-mammals-human"])   # Just one

orfdata proteome --nc-orf-sources all selects every dataset. Evidence presets such as nc_orf_sources="ms" also query every compatible dataset; use nc_orf_sources="bundled" for only the bundled set. They merge after the bundled catalogue, Chang et al.'s before Yang et al.'s as for mouse, so an ORF in several keeps the first one's ID. Together they give 69,286 ORFs, of which 69,162 place on Ensembl 115; that takes about a minute and several GB of memory, against about a second for the bundled catalogue alone. Neither adds MS evidence, so "ms" selects the same ORFs either way.

  • ncorf-mammals-human: the human ncORFs of Chang et al., from 174 Ribo-seq libraries (Table S1), built as for mouse on Ensembl 107 GRCh38: 11,621 of the source's 11,623, two having a coding length that isn't their protein plus a stop. Types: uORF (6,178), lncORF (2,231), uoORF (1,633), iORF (773), dORF (694) and doORF (112); 997 start at GTG.
  • riborf-human: the human ORFs of Yang et al., from 136 samples in 30 GEO series, on GENCODE V39, placed through the same Ensembl 105 transcripts (GENCODE V39 is Ensembl 105): 62,853 of 62,962 non-skipped rows; 109 are on transcripts with no sequence in Ensembl 105's FASTAs. The catalogue includes 11,679 valid records below five residues. Types: uORF (28,981), lncORF (12,938), iORF (5,990), dORF (4,907), uoORF (4,679), N-terminal truncation (3,574), extension (1,046) and doORF (738).

catalogs takes None (the species' default set), "all", or catalogue names, "bundled" among them. orfdata catalogs status marks optional catalogues. Everywhere but human, every catalogue is in the default set.

docs.title: Zebrafish, C. elegans and yeast
docs.text:
orfdata setup --species zebrafish   # or worm, or yeast

Yang et al.'s RibORF 2.0 ORFs of the mouse catalogue's kind, including valid short source models, from each species' sheet of Supplementary Data 3, imported the same way:

Catalogue Samples (GEO series) Placed through ORFs Below 5 aa riborf-zebrafish 20 (2) Ensembl 115 GRCz11 transcripts 15,491 5,732 riborf-worm 39 (1) Ensembl 105 WBcel235 transcripts 4,035 1,186 riborf-yeast 5 (1) the R64-1-1 genome (sacCer3) 1,369 241
  • Zebrafish: every source transcript has the same length in Ensembl 100 to 115, so the catalogue uses 115. 18 rows have ambiguous bases in the ORF and are left out. Types: uORF (6,168), N-terminal truncation (3,816), iORF (2,696), dORF (1,623), lncORF (501), uoORF (343), extension (224) and doORF (120).
  • C. elegans: the source's transcripts match Ensembl 100 and 105, and WormBase changed many models after, so the catalogue uses 105; all 4,035 place there. Transcript names with dots of their own (F45H11.11.1) are kept whole. Types: iORF (1,525), uORF (725), truncation (614), extension (556), lncORF (158), uoORF (249), doORF (121) and dORF (87).
  • Yeast: the source's yeast transcripts carry UTRs, and some are unstable transcripts (CUTs, SUTs), none of which Ensembl's yeast annotation has; its transcripts span only the CDS. So each ORF is placed from its genomic span and translated from the pinned genome. The source gives block sizes but not starts, so the 4 ORFs on two exons are rebuilt from their first block's size at the start and last block's at the end, each across a GT-AG intron; Ty1's programmed frameshift (YNL284C-B, two blocks 1 nt apart) is left out. A record names the Ensembl transcript (YNL046W_mRNA) only when that transcript carries its coding path; otherwise it names the source's transcript (YNR004W, CUT808), with the Ensembl gene where there is one. Only the 171 ORFs on an Ensembl transcript, such as truncations and iORFs, place on a PyEnsembl genome; the rest (uORFs in 5′ UTRs, ORFs on CUTs) stay in the catalogue, queryable by region and gene, until ORFs on source-defined RNAs are supported (#66). Types: uORF (393), dORF (267), lncORF (260), iORF (139), truncation (138), extension (67), uoORF (58) and doORF (47).

docs.title: Dog
docs.text:
No public resource gives dog ORF-level translation evidence, as of October 2026:

  • Ribo-seq. No dog ribosome profiling is in GEO, SRA or ENA, and none of OpenProt, RiboSeq.org (147 organisms), RPFdb, SmProt or GWIPS-viz has dog. The one dog experiment published, Pfeffer et al. 2015 (canine pancreas rough-ER microsomes), deposited no reads.
  • Mass spectrometry. Every dog dataset searched canonical proteins only, so none reports a noncanonical peptide as deposited: the Canine PeptideAtlas (PXD052932, 149,546 peptides from 13 tissues, plasma and urine), the dog tumour DLA immunopeptidome (PXD074485, 12,948 distinct database-search ligands), the Pfizer TMT atlas (PXD070290) and the dog brain proteome (PXD033420, PXD034449). The first two are available as dog peptide datasets, as evidence for known proteins.

Dog ncORF evidence therefore needs those spectra searched again against dog ORF sequences. Human and mouse ORFs are never transferred to dog by orthology. Dog proteomes contain their PyEnsembl-annotated proteins, and dog RNA, protein abundance and peptides are available as measurements.

docs.title: Every assembly of a species
docs.text:
Catalogues on another assembly of the species are lifted automatically. Download the pinned chain files once, and load_catalog, extra_orfs(genome) and Proteome.build(genome, nc_orf_sources="ms") work on every human and mouse assembly PyEnsembl knows:

orfdata chains download --accept-terms   # Every pinned chain; without --accept-terms, UCSC's mouse ones are skipped

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import Proteome

Proteome.build(EnsemblRelease(75), nc_orf_sources="ms")  # GRCh37: the GRCh38 catalogue, lifted

With evidence None (every catalogue ORF), each assembly gets:

Genome ORF source Records Placed Not placed: main reasons Human Ensembl 115, GRCh38 bundled 7,264 7,239 24 splice paths changed Human Ensembl 75, GRCh37 lifted, 1 hop 7,247 6,857 270 transcripts absent, 108 paths changed, 1 on a transcript with a different protein Human Ensembl 54, NCBI36 lifted, 1 hop 7,253 4,195 2,708 transcripts absent, 2 on a transcript with a different protein Human Ensembl rapid 2022_07, T2T-CHM13v2.0 lifted, 1 hop 7,208 6,767 383 on a transcript with a different protein, 58 on no transcript, 56 not lifted Mouse Ensembl 115, GRCm39 OpenProt, Chang et al. and Yang et al. 60,707 60,475 232 fail transcript/path/sequence binding checks

Older annotations lack many of the transcripts the sources name, so fewer ORFs place; the rest, and any that didn't lift, are listed with the reason, never silently dropped.

  • Which catalogues. Every catalogue for the species is used, merged: on the requested assembly as is, on the others the pinned chains reach, lifted. Each contributes one release: the one on the requested assembly if it has one, else its default. The requested assembly's come first, then by fewest hops; bundled first, then by the registry's priority, which decides whose ID a shared ORF keeps, so a new catalogue never renames existing ORFs. A source already used from a nearer assembly, such as one catalogue registered again under another name on another assembly, counts once. This depends only on the registry and the pinned chains, never on what happens to be installed.
  • What's missing. Missing catalogues and chain files are reported together, each with the command that installs it; nothing is downloaded while loading. cache_root (or --cache-root) is where both are looked for.
  • Your own catalogues. extra_orfs(genome, catalog=...) and Proteome.build(genome, nc_orf_sources=catalog) lift a catalogue, or each of a list, that is on another assembly of the species through the same chains.
  • Other names. Assemblies go by Ensembl's names. hg38, GRCh38.p14, mm39 and the like get an error that names the assembly to use, and a custom genome needs that reference_name.
  • Routes. chain_routes(species, build) gives the fewest-hop route to each assembly the pinned chains reach, for example GRCm39 to NCBIM37 through GRCm38. lift_to(catalog, build) lifts through it. catalog_status() lists, for each catalogue, the assemblies it reaches and whether their chains are downloaded.
  • Cost. Lifting takes a few seconds (about 2 s for the human catalogue to GRCh37 or CHM13); a process reuses the result for the same installed catalogues and chains.
  • Unlifted ORFs. ExtraORFs.unlifted lists the ORFs the evidence rule selects that a lift left out; proteomes count them as unlifted and list them among their exclusions. ExtraORFs.excluded holds only records of its catalogue, which is what Varcode looks up.

docs.title: T2T-CHM13
docs.text:
PyEnsembl's EnsemblRelease has no T2T-CHM13 annotation, so orfdata pins Ensembl's rapid-release one (2022_07) and installs it on request, checking each file's size and SHA-256. The T2T Consortium's GRCh38-to-CHM13 chain is public domain (CC0):

orfdata genomes install t2t-chm13          # 143 MB of Ensembl files, plus about 1.1 GB of PyEnsembl index
orfdata chains download GRCh38 T2T-CHM13v2.0
orfdata proteome --genome t2t-chm13 --nc-orf-sources ms --output chm13.fasta

from orfdata import Proteome, load_genome

genome = load_genome("t2t-chm13")          # A PyEnsembl Genome named T2T-CHM13v2.0, offline
proteome = Proteome.build(genome, nc_orf_sources="ms")  # 104,957 reference proteins + 2,039 MS-supported ORFs

The bundled GRCh38 catalogue lifts automatically: 7,208 of 7,264 ORFs lift, and 6,767 place on CHM13 transcripts with their exact coding path and protein. Ensembl gave CHM13 transcripts new IDs, so placement is by path. Of the 441 that don't place, 383 lie on a CHM13 transcript with their exact coding path whose sequence, from CHM13's own alleles, encodes a different protein (in 15, the start codon itself differs); the exclusion reason names that transcript. The other 58 are on no CHM13 transcript. The genome keeps its species and assembly accession when pickled, for multiprocessing and Varcode. Your own CHM13 genome works too if its reference_name is T2T-CHM13v2.0 and it has a species (or you pass context=); hs1 or chm13 get an error saying so.

docs.title: Lifting a catalogue by hand
docs.text:
orfdata lift writes a lifted catalogue to a file, for any route the pinned chains cover or with your own chain file:

orfdata lift --species human --to GRCh37 --output orfs-grch37.json.gz

  "lifted": "orfdata-catalog:2026-10-11.1@GRCh37",
  ...
  "lifted_records": 7247,
  "unmapped": 17,
  "unmapped_reasons": {
    "A coding block crosses an alignment gap or edge": 2,
    "A coding block is not aligned": 15
  },

orfdata lift writes the lifted catalogue and prints a summary to standard error. --catalog FILE lifts a local catalogue instead, and --chain FILE uses your own chain file instead of a downloaded pin. Pass the result back with --nc-orf-sources for orfdata proteome; JSON and TSV exports include each record's original and the chain. In Python:

from orfdata import download_chain, lift_catalog, load_catalog, load_chain

download_chain("GRCh38", "GRCh37")  # Once; checksum-verified. download_chains() gets them all.
grch37 = lift_catalog(load_catalog(), load_chain("GRCh38", "GRCh37"))
grch37.save("orfs-grch37.json.gz")
print(len(grch37.records), len(grch37.metadata["liftover"]["unmapped"]), grch37.source)

7247 17 orfdata-catalog:2026-10-11.1@GRCh37
  • Pinned chain files. The T2T Consortium's GRCh38 to and from T2T-CHM13v2.0 are public domain. Ensembl's human GRCh38 to and from GRCh37 and NCBI36, and mouse GRCm38 to and from NCBIM37, have no usage restrictions. orfdata chains list shows all ten. UCSC's mouse mm10ToMm39 and mm39ToMm10 (GRCm38 and GRCm39) are free only for non-commercial use, so downloading them needs --accept-terms (accept_terms=True). --source-path FILE installs a copy you already have after checking it against the pin. Ensembl publishes no GRCm38/GRCm39 chain, and no chain is pinned for dog.
  • Other chain files. ChainFile(path, source_build=..., target_build=...) reads any UCSC or Ensembl chain file, gzipped or not. A chain file doesn't name its assemblies, so you declare them. When the file is one of the pinned ones, its direction and species are checked, so a GRCh37-to-GRCh38 file can't lift a GRCh38 catalogue; any other file is taken at your word. UCSC's chains to GCF assemblies, such as canFam3ToGCF_014441545.1.over.chain.gz for dog ROS_Cfam_1.0, name contigs by RefSeq accession, so pass contig_names= built from NCBI's assembly report to match the genome's names. Check each file's terms before using or sharing what it produces.
  • What lifts. A record lifts only when every coding block lies inside one ungapped alignment block and all blocks land on one contig and strand, in order. Where a region also aligns to fix patches or alternate haplotypes, the same-named chromosome is used. The 17 bundled ORFs above that don't lift are listed in metadata["liftover"]["unmapped"] with the reason (and, when a block aligns to several places, their contigs): 15 have no alignment and 2 cross an alignment gap. UCSC's names for unplaced scaffolds, such as chr1_GL456210v1_random, are read as Ensembl's (GL456210.1).
  • Real data. Lifting the 7,247 back to GRCh38 with GRCh37_to_GRCh38.chain.gz recovers the original coordinates of the 7,246 that lift back. On Ensembl 75, 6,857 of the lifted ORFs place on a transcript with their exact coding path and protein.
  • Provenance. Each lifted record keeps its original in record.lifted_from and the chain's file name and SHA-256 in record.liftover, the same whether the file was downloaded as a pin or passed by hand. Its ID, protein and evidence must equal the original's. Its initiation flanks move with it when they map consistently and in order. A strain pin is kept, with the chain's SHA-256 in place of an annotation. metadata["liftover"]["input"] describes the input catalogue, including any earlier lift. ORFCatalog.save writes the same bytes for the same catalogue.
  • Placement. extra_orfs on the target genome then checks each ORF's exact coding path and protein, so a lift that changes the sequence is excluded rather than trusted. A lifted record names no annotation release. ORFs that didn't lift are reported among the exclusions, as "Did not lift to GRCh37: …", when the evidence rule selects them; through every hop of an earlier lift and every merged input. On Ensembl 75, "ms" selects all 2,186 MS-supported ORFs: 2,097 place, and 3 of the 89 excluded didn't lift.
  • Size. Each lifted record carries its original, so a lifted catalogue is about twice the size of its input (33 MB for the bundled one as JSON).
  • Errors. When no pinned chains reach an assembly, such as HG002, load_catalog(species=..., genome_build=...) gives the orfdata lift --chain command and the Python call that lifts with your own chain file.

docs.title: Source builds
docs.text:
registry.build(name, source_paths={"source.json": path}) explicitly rebuilds an allowlisted source adapter. registry.open_build(name) opens that local result, and inspect_build(name) checks its input pins, transform identity and output receipt without reopening original input files. The CLI equivalents are catalogs build NAME --source-path source.json=PATH and catalogs query NAME --built. A local receipt's checksum is distinct from an independently pinned published artifact; inspect_build().verified remains false.

Builds are atomic. force=True creates a fresh bundle while existing readers' files survive. Cache roots follow ORFDATA_CACHE, OPENVAX_DATA_CACHE, or the explicit cache_root; catalogues, quantitative datasets and local source builds use separate locations.

docs.title: Defining a release
docs.text:
A registry definition maps a name to default_version, versions and an optional integer priority (default 100): when catalogues are merged, lower priorities come first, and the first catalogue's ID names an ORF several share. Each version contains a CatalogManifest, distribution access terms and an assets entry for raw catalog.json.gz bytes, pinned by URL, SHA-256 and size. The manifest declares references, original SourceAsset inputs, citations, processing and coverage. coverage.records is required; source importers also report original assignment counts and unresolved categories. Distinct protein sequences and evidence summaries are separate counts.

Managed files use the existing orfdata.catalog.v1 JSON representation and embed the full manifest in metadata.catalog_manifest. Every accepted record must declare a complete genomic reference included in that manifest. Opening validates the whole manifest, species/assembly, references and declared output counts.

The initial catalog-copy-v1 adapter wraps an independently prepared, unmanaged, pinned portable catalogue named by processing.catalog_asset; it preserves native metadata and adds the managed manifest. It rejects an input that already has a managed manifest instead of replacing its release provenance. It does not infer missing references or validate new biological models on behalf of a source importer.

Python developers can use build_catalog(manifest, builder), where builder(inputs, output_path) writes the managed file. DataCache verifies inputs and validates the completed output before publishing the local build. Importer paths in metadata are never executed as Python code.

OpenProt source qualification and its coordinate discrepancy remain separate from this data-management API.

The pinned files contain transcript/protein sequences, not chromosome DNA. For intronic sequence and structural products, explicitly install the consortium's CHM13v2.0 chromosome FASTA:

orfdata genomes install t2t-chm13 --genome-fasta https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/human-pangenomics/T2T/CHM13/assemblies/analysis_set/chm13v2.0.fa.gz

from orfdata import load_genome

dna = "https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/human-pangenomics/T2T/CHM13/assemblies/analysis_set/chm13v2.0.fa.gz"
genome = load_genome("t2t-chm13", genome_fasta_path_or_url=dna)
sequence = genome.sequence("1", 1, 100)  # 1-based inclusive; offline after install

A local chromosome FASTA path works too. Supply the same source when loading; DNA is optional and is not silently added to annotation-only loads. This DNA source is caller-selected, separate from the checksum-pinned annotation assets. Allow roughly 1 GB for the compressed download and several GB for installed DNA and indexes. Loading never downloads DNA. Missing DNA raises an installation error when accessed. Species taxonomy and nuclear/mitochondrial genetic codes are retained in PyEnsembl's saved reference metadata.

docs.title: Yeast protein and RNA abundance
docs.text:
copy-yeast-abundance imports Lawless et al., CoPY (2016) through the same dataset API as human, mouse and dog. It includes calibrated protein and peptide quantities, label-free estimates and RNA from budding yeast grown in glucose-limited chemostats. The strain is EUROSCARF Y11335 BY4742, with the reported genotype retained on each sample.

pip install 'orfdata'
orfdata datasets info copy-yeast-abundance
orfdata datasets download copy-yeast-abundance
orfdata datasets pairs copy-yeast-abundance --basis condition_aggregate

The release contains 69,125 observations in a roughly 14 MB compressed download (168 MB installed). Downloads are explicit and checksum-verified through DataCache. Queries work offline after installation.

Source measurements Coverage Interpretation QconCAT SRM protein summaries 1,903 rows 1,167 quantified; 668 upper bounds; 68 unquantifiable SRM peptide observations 3,836 rows × four cultures and author median Protein-specific isotope standards; copies/cell, classification and uncertainty Aggregate RNA 6,581 labels × FPKM and estimated copies/cell Counts aggregated before FPKM; copies assume 60,000 total mRNAs/cell Individual RNA libraries Four × 7,137 tracking IDs Native FPKM, 95% confidence interval and Cufflinks status Label-free estimates 3,166 rows × two methods Q-Exactive internal-standard Top3 and SAX total-protein scaling remain separate

The 55 joined SRM protein groups retain their combined attribution. Label-free identities also remain groups because full membership is unresolved. Two rows share the label YNL239W; both survive unchanged. Upper bounds have status="below_detection", value=None and a detection_limit; missing and unquantifiable values never become zeros. Author-calibrated SRM estimates have origin="observed"; the RNA copies/cell conversion has origin="derived" with its original FPKM input and calibration assumption.

The QconCAT FASTA contains 93 synthetic calibration standards, not native yeast proteins. Four reported peptides do not match their assigned standard; their measurements retain an explicit validation flag. See source reconciliation #34. Raw transitions and light/heavy ratios are not supplied in the processed workbook. SRM raw data are identified by PASS00717; PXD002694 is the label-free deposit. RNA is from GSE73898. Cufflinks LOWDATA rows retain their original positive/zero estimates and confidence bounds in provenance, while the query value remains not_measured because reliable quantification is unresolved.

docs.title: Comparing RNA and protein
docs.text:
The paper supports same-cell measurements at the source-cohort level. The individual MS-to-RNA replicate crosswalk is unresolved, so comparisons require explicit condition_aggregate selection. Replicate numbers alone never join samples. Label-free methods have different calibrations and no inferred RNA pair.

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry

dataset = DatasetRegistry().open("copy-yeast-abundance")
match = next(
    m for m in dataset.matched_measurements(allowed_bases=["condition_aggregate"])
    if m.relation.left.identifier == "YML035C"  # AMD1, yeast source context
)
protein = match.right[0]  # 3203.943997 copies/cell; author SRM estimate
rna = next(m for m in match.left if m.unit == "copies/cell")  # ~2.11665
ratio = match.ratio(
    protein, rna, measurement_id="AMD1:protein-per-RNA",
    method="native calibrated protein / estimated RNA",
    normalization={"assumed_total_mrna_per_cell": 60000, "level": "source cohort"},
)
print(ratio.value, ratio.unit, ratio.derivation)

The ratio is conditional on the RNA calibration. It is neither a translation rate nor ribosome occupancy. Group relationships cannot yield an individual protein ratio. All quantities keep their source units and assumptions.

docs.title: References and other species
docs.text:
Both yeast contexts carry taxon 4932 and pinned source hashes. The historical SGD/Bowtie genome and annotation releases are unspecified; assembly, annotation version and reference strain remain null. These source labels support canonical gene/protein relationships but cannot bind a current PyEnsembl transcript until a reference mapping is validated. Sample BY4742 strain is separate from the unknown reference-genome strain. This dataset does not establish which yeast noncanonical ORFs were searched, expressed or absent.

For cross-species comparisons, supply independently validated, pinned orthology records rather than joining gene names. For example, with an installed mammal RNA dataset and a curated JSON list of OrthologyMapping records:

import json
from orfdata import OrthologyMapping, compare_orthologs

with open("curated-yeast-mammal-orthology.json") as handle:
    mappings = [OrthologyMapping.from_dict(row) for row in json.load(handle)]
for comparison in compare_orthologs(dataset, mammal_rna_dataset, mappings):
    print(comparison.left, comparison.right)  # Separate original measurements

The mapping must name both exact references, its release, source checksum, cardinality and confidence. No expression or protein-existence evidence transfers between species, and different cultures/calibrations remain different experiments. See pairing and orthology.

To rebuild the release from the pinned public workbook, standards, metadata and four RNA files, install orfdata and run orfdata datasets build copy-yeast-abundance. Python uses DatasetRegistry().build("copy-yeast-abundance"). Local verified inputs can be supplied with repeated --source-path ASSET=PATH or source_paths={...}. The workbook and standards use stable versioned PMC objects; the dynamically generated EuropePMC ZIP is not used as a content identity.

docs.title: Released data and gaps
docs.text:
ORFdata keeps datasets in separate species/reference contexts and exposes them through the same discovery, download and query API. This table describes actual data coverage, independently of what the API can represent.

Species RNA abundance Protein abundance RNA/protein pairing Human Wang: 29 specimens, gene/transcript FPKM and estimated copies/cell Wang: 15,210 groups, iBAQ and estimated copies/cell; Pfizer: 10,352 groups, 37 channels, iBAQ/rIBAQ Wang: adjacent cryosections; Pfizer: native RNA missing Mouse Pfizer: 606 libraries, 56,051 gene targets, counts Pfizer: 12,124 groups, 63 channels, iBAQ/rIBAQ Unresolved library-to-pool correspondence Dog Pfizer: 434 libraries, 30,941 gene targets, counts; mammary stroma: 18,582 genes × 30 samples Pfizer: 9,929 groups, 38 channels, iBAQ/rIBAQ; mammary stroma: 1,583 native groups × 28 samples Mammary stroma: 14 shared specimens, 28 paired compartments and two RNA samples without protein mates; Pfizer crosswalk remains unresolved Budding yeast CoPY: four RNA libraries plus a source aggregate, FPKM and estimated copies/cell; Ingolia: four RNA libraries, counts and densities CoPY: calibrated SRM and separately calibrated label-free estimates CoPY: explicit source-cohort pairing; individual cross-assay replicate matches unknown

docs.title: Peptides and MHC ligands
docs.text:
Dog has four peptide-level datasets:

  • Mammary stroma (guide): 5,413 native peptide rows, intensity and LFQ columns, reported group memberships and original control/decoy flags across 28 samples.
  • Pfizer native peptide evidence (guide): 953,980 target peptide sequences, native peptide/PSM reporter quantities and reported protein-group memberships. The 96 runs retain 38 tissue pools, four bridge channels and two empty channels; source memberships and searched-FASTA candidates stay separate.
  • Canine PeptideAtlas (guide, build 573): 149,546 tryptic peptides with PSM counts in 18 Labrador tissue, plasma and urine samples, every protein location, and 17,795 protein calls, 17,110 of them mapped to Ensembl 110 proteins with an identical sequence. PeptideAtlas states no licence, so this dataset is built locally from its download and never redistributed.
  • DLA class I ligands (guide, Kaabinejadian et al.): 76,550 PEAKS rows from four dog tumours, each searched against four protein databases, and from three human HCT 116 lines that each express one DLA-88 allele.

All four searched known proteins only. Other species have no peptide-level measurement dataset yet; the human and mouse ORF catalogues carry pooled peptide evidence for their noncanonical ORFs.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
• Gene targets include measured zeros; their presence in a matrix does not imply expression in every sample.
  • Protein-group representatives do not establish unique protein attribution.
  • TMT channels are not independent donors.
  • Wang processing views do not add specimens, and gene-level comparisons do not resolve individual protein isoforms or noncanonical ORFs.

Calibration and uncertainty remain attached to observations:

  • CoPY RNA copies/cell assume 60,000 total mRNAs. Its 1,903 SRM summaries contain 1,167 point estimates, 668 upper bounds and 68 unquantifiable results.
  • Human Wang protein copies use the proteomic-ruler estimate; RNA copies assume mRNA is 2% of total RNA mass. These calibrations remain distinct from yeast isotope-standard measurements.

docs.title: ORF evidence and ribosome profiling
docs.text:
The separate existence-evidence catalogue contains 7,264 human noncanonical ORFs, including 2,186 with reported MS support. Mouse has 60,707 ORFs: Ribo-seq ORFs from Chang et al. and Yang et al., and 2,976 OpenProt 2.2 ORFs with at least two unique MS peptides, built from their sources' files. Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq ORFs cover zebrafish (15,491), C. elegans (4,035) and yeast (1,369), and with Chang et al.'s are optional human catalogues; dog has no experimental ncORF catalogue, because no dog Ribo-seq or ncORF MS search is public (details). Its ribosome evidence and pooled PSM counts are not sample-level ribosome occupancy or protein abundance.

The separate Ingolia yeast release contains four Ribo-seq libraries across 13,748 source regions, alongside four RNA libraries. Exact region coordinates and RNA/RPF aliquot pairing remain unresolved. Other species do not yet have released quantitative Ribo-seq datasets in this registry.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text: See the short guides for matched human tissues, protein measurements, native dog/mouse RNA, yeast RNA/protein calibration, yeast RNA/ribosome occupancy and complete search sequences. The roadmap tracks further human comparators, quantitative Ribo-seq, ncORF evidence and additional species. Cat, cattle, rat and other taxa use the same model when source datasets are added. Orthology comparisons are explicit and never transfer observations or protein-existence evidence between species.

docs.title: Canine paired measurements and translation-evidence audit
docs.text: Source check: 28 October 2026. This audit identifies importable measurement files and their limitations. The subsequent mammary-stroma importer now exposes the paired study through the common quantitative registry. The machine-readable audit contains source URLs, hashes, counts, search queries and a candidate sample crosswalk.

docs.title: Paired RNA and protein: a verified study
docs.text:
Amini et al., 2021 studied cancer-associated and normal stroma from archived canine mammary carcinomas. The authors explicitly reused the cases of their earlier RNA study. Original case 7 was excluded from proteomics because its paraffin block was unavailable. Measurements come from separate laser-capture preparations of the same tissue cases, not identical RNA/protein aliquots.

Source Verified processed data Download GSE135183 18,582 genes × 30 RNA samples, 15 cases with two stromal compartments Raw counts, 606 KB compressed PXD023023 1,583 native protein-group rows with 28 LFQ sample columns Protein groups, 2.8 MB PXD023023 5,413 peptide rows with native quantitative fields Peptides, 4.5 MB

The downloaded protein and peptide files match PRIDE's deposited SHA-1 checksums; the audit also records SHA-256 for all three processed files. RNA values are nonnegative integer counts. Native protein-group counts include controls and contaminants and are not counts of confidently detected biological proteins.

PRIDE filenames use case numbers 1–15; GEO uses case IDs such as 109 and 135. Matching the article's Table 1 to GEO by breed, age and histological subtype uniquely reconciles all 14 proteomics cases. The resulting 28 sample links are metadata-derived, not an author-supplied identifier crosswalk. Breed spelling normalizations are recorded. GEO case 127 is the unmatched RNA case.

An importer must retain that pairing basis, separate stromal compartments, protein-group ambiguity, controls, missing quantities and native units. The deposited search used a dated canonical UniProt reference, but its FASTA is not among the 31 PRIDE files. Sequence/reference qualification remains necessary; these data do not establish ncORF translation. Author-derived contrasts in the supplementary workbooks must stay distinct from sample-level measurements. The paired study is now imported as canine-mammary-stroma; the remaining dog data requests stay tracked in #20.

docs.title: Dog Ribo-seq and ncORF translation
docs.text:
The date-stamped dog-specific SRA, GEO and ENA queries in the audit returned no matching sequencing records. This is a bounded repository search, not proof that no unpublished or differently indexed experiment exists.

Pfeffer et al., 2015 reports ribosome profiling and total RNA sequencing of canine pancreas rough-ER preparations aligned to CanFam3.1/Ensembl 77. Its accession section lists EMDB and PDB deposits, without a sequencing accession. No downloadable reads or processed ORF-level counts were verified in this audit. Even if recovered, the preparation would describe an enriched pancreatic compartment, not a broad normal-tissue canine translatome.

Existing canine PeptideAtlas, Pfizer and DLA datasets retain their deposited canonical-search scope. The experimental dog ncORF search pipeline is a route to new analysis, not a released experimentally supported catalogue. Dog ncORF translation coverage therefore remains unavailable pending qualified data or a separately validated reanalysis. See #12.

docs.title: Dog peptides: MHC ligands and the Canine PeptideAtlas
docs.text:
Two dog peptide datasets record which peptides of known dog proteins mass spectrometry has observed. Neither searched for noncanonical ORFs, so they don't add ORFs to the dog proteome (why dog has no ncORF catalogue).

For a verified paired RNA/protein study and the latest bounded search for dog Ribo-seq, see the canine source audit.

Dataset What it holds How to get it kaabinejadian-dog-dla-ligands DLA class I ligands from four dog tumours and three DLA-88 monoallelic cell lines orfdata datasets download (CC0, 25 MB) peptideatlas-dog-peptides 149,546 tryptic peptides from 18 Labrador tissue, plasma and urine samples, with genome locations orfdata datasets build (built locally from 71 MB of sources)

docs.title: DLA class I ligands
docs.text:
Kaabinejadian et al. (2026) eluted peptides from DLA class I molecules with the BB7.6 or H58A antibody. PRIDE PXD074485 deposits their PEAKS Studio 11.5 peptide tables (1% FDR), which this dataset imports in full: 76,550 rows, each with its PEAKS area, intensity and spectrum count.

Sample Tumour Breed DLA-88 typing Antibodies Lola osteosarcoma Black Russian Terrier *501:01 BB7.6, H58A 163828A anal sac adenocarcinoma English Cocker Spaniel *004:02 BB7.6 Lily anal sac adenocarcinoma English Cocker Spaniel *501:01, *501:02, *004:02 H58A Bogey oral melanoma American Cocker Spaniel *003:02, *006:01, *017:01 BB7.6 HCT116-DLA88… human HCT 116 cells, one DLA-88 allele each — *003:02, *012:01 or *501:01 BB7.6

Each tumour's spectra were searched four times: against UniProt's dog proteome, Basenji and Great Dane (Zoey) Ensembl 104 proteins, and a merged database of four dog assemblies. Each search is its own assay (Lola-BB76:UniProt9615, Lola-BB76:MergedCanFams, ...). A peptide found in two searches of one sample is one observation, not two. The HCT 116 lines were searched against human SwissProt, and their peptides are human proteins, so they sit in the dataset's separate human reference context.

Database search finds 11,363 distinct dog peptides in the UniProt searches and 12,948 across all four databases, leaving out iRT standards (below). For the cell lines, the counts of unique 8–14-mers from database search (591 for DLA-88*003:02, 1,465 for *501:01) match the article's. The article's tumour counts come from its curated supplementary lists, which aren't imported (they are CC BY-NC-ND), and match no single table.

Every row keeps its PEAKS identification type in provenance as found_by: DB Search, DeepNovo (de novo sequencing) or Homolog (SPIDER homology search). Only database-search peptides are guaranteed to occur in a listed protein, so filter on it for a conservative ligand list.

docs.title: iRT standards
docs.text:
Every run was spiked with Biognosys iRT retention-time peptides, and their spectra appear in every search, often in disguise. 10,629 rows are marked irt_standard, and irt_rule names the first rule that marked them:

irt_rule Rows Marks a row that irt_sequence 1,179 is a kit peptide or a fragment of one, with I and L equal kit_only 1,097 PEAKS attributes only to the kit (homology reads of kit peptides) irt_precursor 1,276 sits at the precursor of a row marked by the first two rules in the same immunoprecipitation: same charge, m/z within 20 ppm, retention time within a minute de_novo_irt 7,077 is a de novo sequence that PEAKS matches to the kit, or that shares 6 or more consecutive residues with a kit peptide

The precursor rule applies to de novo and homology rows. It applies to database-search rows only in the merged database, which lacks the kit, and only when no search with the kit found the same peptide. Elsewhere PEAKS could choose the kit peptide and didn't.

  • De novo rows: half of them (8,448 of 16,830) are iRT reads, often a kit peptide with residues added or changed (KATLFLQFGAQGSPFLK). Don't take an unmarked de novo sequence for a new ligand without checking its spectrum.
  • Homology rows: 8 are marked by precursor, such as TGFLLDPVLNR, which has exactly the mass of GTFIIDPGGVIR and co-elutes with it.
  • Database-search rows: apart from 1,075 kit peptides, only one is marked: IFLAFQQKAYVAP, matched to dog proteins in the merged database at the precursor of LFLQFGAAGSPFLK.
  • Chance matches: few. Shuffled kit sequences share 6 residues with about 3 de novo rows, and shifting the kit's retention times by 10–20 minutes puts about 14 de novo rows at a kit precursor.

A mapping is unmapped when any of its rows is marked. Release 2026-10-16.1 (importer kaabinejadian-dla-v1) marked only exact kit sequences and kit-only attributions (2,242 rows), so it missed the disguised reads.

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()
ligands = registry.open("kaabinejadian-dog-dla-ligands")  # After downloading it.
dog = next(r for r in ligands.manifest.references if r.taxon_id == 9615)

# Where a peptide was eluted, and how it was identified.
peptide = ScopedTarget(dog, "peptide", "AIKKGLEEL", "amino-acid-sequence")
for m in ligands.measurements(target=peptide, quantity="spectrum_count"):
    print(m.sample_id, m.assay_id, m.value, m.provenance["found_by"])

# Lola's database-search ligands (BB7.6, UniProt search).
lola = {m.target.identifier for m in ligands.measurements(
            reference=dog, assay_id="Lola-BB76:UniProt9615", quantity="spectrum_count")
        if m.provenance["found_by"] == "DB Search" and not m.provenance["irt_standard"]}

# Why a row is marked as an iRT standard.
for m in ligands.measurements(target=peptide, quantity="spectrum_count"):
    print(m.assay_id, m.provenance["irt_standard"], m.provenance["irt_rule"])

Targets are unmodified sequences; each row's modified form (for example M(+15.99)) is in its provenance as peptide. mappings() lists, for each search and identification type, the proteins PEAKS reported for a peptide: unique or ambiguous for database-search and homology matches, and unmapped with a reason for iRT standards and de novo sequences, whose listed proteins stay in the mapping's evidence. The search FASTAs weren't deposited, so no accession can be checked against a sequence.

docs.title: Runs missing from the deposit
docs.text:
PEAKS reports, for each peptide, the raw file and scan of its best spectrum, and sums its spectra and area over all of the sample's runs. The authors' PEAKS projects for two immunoprecipitations included runs that the deposit lacks, so each row records raw_file_deposited. For 1,695 rows the best spectrum comes from a missing run:

  • Lily (H58A): a second injection of the remaining eluate, 22-1107 "1uL Residue" (fractions 12–30), 299 rows. The first injection, 22-1104, is deposited.
  • DLA-88*012:01: the 20240929 acquisition (fractions 14–25), 1,396 of its 1,635 rows. The line's archive holds only its 20241013 runs (fractions 26–28 in triplicate, and blanks), though the SDRF names the 20240929 run as the assay.

Those identifications come from the authors' tables, but their spectra can't be checked against the deposit. The raw files of 163828A's H58A run have no deposited results and aren't included.

docs.title: Canine PeptideAtlas
docs.text:
The Canine PeptideAtlas (Kusebauch et al. 2026) reprocessed 138 runs from Labrador Retrievers (13 tissues, plasma and urine; PRIDE PXD052932) at a PSM FDR of 0.001. This dataset imports its 2024-01 build (573):

  • PSM counts for 149,546 peptides in each of the 18 samples where they were observed (528,272 values);
  • every protein each peptide maps to, with its position and, for Ensembl proteins, its ROS_Cfam_1.0 coordinates (exon-spanning peptides have one location per exon);
  • the build's 17,795 protein calls with presence levels (6,423 canonical). Of its 17,307 UniProt and Ensembl calls, 16,959 map to one Ensembl 110 protein with an identical sequence, 151 to several and 197 to none; contaminant and decoy calls aren't mapped.

PeptideAtlas states no licence for its downloads, so orfdata never redistributes this dataset. build downloads the build's 61 MB export and Ensembl 110's dog proteins, checks their SHA-256, and builds the dataset locally (about a minute; 540 MB on disk). After that, open works offline.

orfdata datasets build peptideatlas-dog-peptides

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

atlas = DatasetRegistry().open("peptideatlas-dog-peptides")  # After building it.
source, ensembl = atlas.manifest.references

# PSMs of one peptide in each sample.
peptide = ScopedTarget(source, "peptide", "AAHEEICTTNEGVMYR", "amino-acid-sequence")
for m in atlas.measurements(target=peptide):
    print(m.sample_id, m.value)

# The PeptideAtlas call for a PyEnsembl dog protein (albumin).
transcript = EnsemblRelease(110, species="dog").transcript_by_id("ENSCAFT00845010439")
protein = ScopedTarget(ensembl, "protein", transcript.protein_id, "ensembl")
for mapped in atlas.mapped_measurements(protein, require_sequence=True):
    call = mapped.measurement
    print(call.target.identifier, call.value, call.provenance["presence_level"])

The ensembl context is exactly PyEnsembl's dog release 110 (ReferenceContext.from_genome(EnsemblRelease(110, species="dog"))), so PyEnsembl protein IDs work directly. The dog RNA dataset uses Ensembl 110 IDs too, in a context that also pins its GTF. Ensembl 105–111 have identical sequences for all 25,710 Ensembl proteins in PeptideAtlas's search set.

Each peptide's mapping (mappings(), keyed by PeptideAtlas accession) keeps its locations as [protein, start, end, chromosome, strand, chromosome_start, chromosome_end, exact]. exact is false for the 4,767 locations where the protein has isoleucine for leucine or the reverse, which PeptideAtlas maps as equal. 204 peptides map only to decoy sequences; they pass the FDR threshold but are probably false identifications, and are unmapped with that reason.

A protein call's PSM count includes peptides it shares with other proteins, so calls don't add up to the build's 13,781,115 PSMs. PeptideAtlas's web page reports 245,884 peptides and 13,716,253 PSMs for the build; its export, which this dataset reproduces, has 149,546 peptides (197,285 distinct modified forms) and 13,781,115 PSMs.

docs.title: Discover and download data
docs.text:
ORFdata has one common entry point for data acquisition:

orfdata data list
orfdata data list --species dog
orfdata data info pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence
orfdata data fetch pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence
orfdata data fetch peptideatlas-dog-peptides openprot-mouse
orfdata data path pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence
orfdata data status

data, downloads and download are aliases for the same command group. The list/info/fetch/path vocabulary follows other OpenVax download tools. fetch accepts one or more explicit resource names and chooses the registered acquisition route: download an artifact when available, otherwise build locally from checksum-pinned source files. All names and required terms are checked before the first acquisition. There is no implicit download-all operation.

info NAME reports the version, source/coverage manifest and distribution metadata, including sizes and redistribution terms where declared. path NAME prints an installed file or directory for scripts; missing data is an error, and never triggers a download. Use --verify on reads to validate local bytes, --cache-root DIR to select a cache, and --json for machine output. fetch --json returns one result per distinct requested name.

Use --kind to disambiguate colliding resource names. For one resource, --version VERSION selects a historical release and --source-path ASSET=PATH provides already downloaded catalogue/dataset sources or genome files. Source overrides remain checksum-checked. --force installs a fresh generation. Restricted chain downloads require --accept-terms after reviewing info.

The same operations are available in Python:

from orfdata import data_info, data_path, fetch_data

details = data_info("openprot-mouse")  # Offline; shows the build route and terms.
result = fetch_data("openprot-mouse")  # Explicit source download and processing.
path = data_path("openprot-mouse")    # Offline file/directory lookup.

The focused forms remain available for additional resource-specific options:

orfdata download viral --species human
orfdata download catalog NAME
orfdata download dataset NAME
orfdata download reference DATASET
orfdata download genome NAME
orfdata download chains --species human

The operation comes first so the same discovery and installation model applies to every resource kind. Focused command groups such as orfdata viral coverage and orfdata viral summary remain useful for domain-specific inspection.

list shows every bundled, downloadable or locally buildable primary resource and its current state, including native protein search references declared by quantitative datasets. status shows resources already usable from local files. Filter either command with --kind or --species; use --installed or --missing with list, --json for programs, and --verify to hash installed files. Discovery and status commands never acquire or repair data.

orfdata download list --kind viral --species human
orfdata download list --missing
orfdata download status --json

Catalogue and dataset releases that cannot be redistributed are built from their pinned sources when selected through orfdata download. The listing's ACQUIRE column says download or build. Existing focused commands such as orfdata catalogs download, orfdata datasets build, orfdata genomes install, and orfdata chains download remain available.

The same inventory is available from Python:

from orfdata import DataStatus, list_data

all_resources: tuple[DataStatus, ...] = list_data()
human_missing: tuple[DataStatus, ...] = list_data(species="human", installed=False)
installed: tuple[DataStatus, ...] = list_data(installed=True)
machine_record: dict[str, object] = all_resources[0].to_dict()

Each DataStatus reports its kind, stable name and version, species, nonexclusive analysis contexts, local status, acquisition method and equivalent command, and resolved cache path. Status values follow DataCache: available, missing, corrupt, or inaccessible. An unknown kind, species or context is an error rather than an empty listing, so a typo never reads as "nothing is available".

docs.title: Viral collections and contexts
docs.text:
The Python API uses the same collection object for discovery, inventory reads, source summaries, downloads and offline opens. The target species comes from the collection; pass species only when you want an explicit consistency check.

from pandas import DataFrame

from orfdata import ViralCollection, viral_collection, viral_collections

human_collections: tuple[ViralCollection, ...] = viral_collections(species="human")
collection: ViralCollection = viral_collection("gdc-viruses")
assert viral_collection(collection.panel) is collection

inventory: DataFrame = collection.inventory()
genbank: DataFrame = collection.source_summary()       # primary source
pave: DataFrame = collection.source_summary("pave")    # another declared source

Names, panel names and aliases resolve through viral_collection() everywhere. An unknown species, collection or source is an error rather than an empty result. A second species is another ViralCollection declaration with its own checked inventory and source summaries; download code does not branch on the species.

The published viral collection currently has these properties:

Property Value Meaning Species human Current target analysis species, NCBI taxon 9606 Collection gdc-viruses Default 200-reference GDC viral screen for human analysis Contexts cancer-transcriptome-screening (cancer) GDC human cancer-transcriptome screening context

Run the default collection with:

orfdata download viral --species human

Viral support is part of a regular pip install orfdata; what needs acquiring is the data. orfdata setup --species human installs this collection along with the human catalogues and chains; --collections none sets up catalogues and chains alone.

--collection gdc-viruses is the default and is available for explicit configuration in scripts that will later choose among several collections. The current collection is for human analysis. A future collection may target another species. Target species does not assert a human source host for every virus. Context is metadata rather than a sequence identity or a mutually exclusive selector. CMV and EBV, for example, may be requested in both cancer and autoimmune workflows. A future collection may carry several context tags, and the same exact accession/version can belong to several collections without becoming several biological references.

Pass --context to materialize a derived FASTA set from the shared source collection. Repeated contexts select their union; --context-match all selects their intersection. It reuses source records already downloaded for the collection, so overlapping contexts do not create conflicting copies of a reference.

orfdata viral contexts
orfdata download viral --context cancer  # all 200 GDC screening references
# Once another listed context is published, select its union or intersection:
orfdata download viral --context cancer-transcriptome-screening --context <another-listed-context>
orfdata download viral --context cancer-transcriptome-screening --context <another-listed-context> --context-match all

The target species is an admission and organization choice for the reference set. It does not replace a source record's viral taxon or assert that the source declared a host. Unknown source-host metadata remains unknown.

The four facts stay separate in the downloaded tables and FASTA headers: the versioned viral accession and CDS feature identify the source product; collection and context record where it was selected; the target species records the analysis it supports; and a source-host taxon is populated only when the source establishes one. This keeps the same reference idempotent when it is obtained through several collections or exporter paths.

The published GDC source inventory is named GRCh38.d1.vd1; gdc-viruses is the ORFdata collection name for its 200 references for human analysis.

Use the full GDC collection for broad screening. For its three cancer selections, list named subsets with orfdata viral subsets:

orfdata download viral --subset cancer-integrated-driver
orfdata download viral --subset cancer-causing
orfdata download viral --subset cancer-associated

cancer-causing is the 20-reference IARC Group 1 selection. cancer-associated is its 37-reference Group 1, 2A and 2B superset. cancer-integrated-driver contains the 12 Group 1 HPV types, HBV, HTLV-1 and MCV. The remaining 163 GDC entries are 162 HPV references outside those IARC tiers plus SV40; their absence from the cancer-associated set does not establish that they are biologically irrelevant. IARC Group 3 means an agent is not classifiable as to carcinogenicity in humans; it is not a safety finding. Future respiratory and autoimmune contexts can overlap the GDC screening context.

docs.title: Three layers, named separately
docs.text:
A downloaded collection keeps the molecular layers apart, and ORFdata uses the same three words everywhere for them:

Layer Molecule Files What it is genome DNA genomes.fasta, genomes.tsv Viral genomic DNA: the same molecules a DNA reference such as GRCh38.d1.vd1 carries as extra contigs transcriptome RNA transcripts.fasta, transcripts.tsv, annotation.gtf One coding transcript per source-annotated CDS feature, spliced, placed on the genome proteome protein proteins.fasta The source translation of each coding transcript

A viral genome is not a transcript and a coding transcript is not a protein, so nothing in the cache mixes them: each layer has its own FASTA, its own identifiers and its own record count. Every transcript also records which source annotated it, and which end, if either, that source marks as running past the record.

from orfdata import open_viral_references

references = open_viral_references(species="human")
for layer in references.layers:
    print(layer.name, layer.molecule, layer.records, layer.fasta)
transcriptome = references.layer("transcriptome")
print(transcriptome.annotation)  # annotation.gtf

Summarize an installed collection, or one selection of it, without writing anything:

orfdata viral summary
orfdata viral summary --subset cancer-causing --json
orfdata viral completeness --incomplete

Because the GTF, transcript FASTA and protein FASTA share identifiers, the set opens as a PyEnsembl genome for downstream variant tools — see Downstream tools.

docs.title: Cache output
docs.text: Downloads have a canonical, versioned path under ORFDATA_CACHE, OPENVAX_DATA_CACHE, or the normal OpenVax cache. This is why the command does not require --output: an arbitrary export path would also need to define resource identity, update and verification behavior. Use --cache-root to put the managed cache elsewhere. The command prints the installed paths; add --json for structured output.

docs.title: Python acquisition convention
docs.text:
ORFdata follows the OpenVax split between explicit acquisition and offline lookup:

from orfdata import ViralReferenceFiles, download_viral_references, open_viral_references

download_viral_references(collection="gdc-viruses")
references: ViralReferenceFiles = open_viral_references(collection="gdc-viruses")

The convenience form is explicit and opt-in:

references = open_viral_references(collection="gdc-viruses", download_if_missing=True)

Context selection is a separate, type-stable API. It returns paths and counts for a derived reference set; it uses the installed collection above and fetches it only when requested:

from orfdata import select_viral_references

cancer = select_viral_references(
    subsets=["cancer-causing"],
    species="human",
    download_if_missing=True,
)

integrated_drivers = select_viral_references(
    subsets=["cancer-integrated-driver"],
    download_if_missing=True,
)

The default is download_if_missing=False, so opening or inspecting a resource does not unexpectedly use the network. The name matches the lower-level PyEnsembl/DataCache convention; high-level PyEnsembl and MHCflurry workflows also expose explicit download or fetch commands.

Across ORFdata download APIs, repeated acquisition reuses a valid installation and force=True refreshes or repairs it, status objects provide to_dict(), human CLI output is the default, and --json provides machine-readable output.

A derived selection is local: select_viral_references(force=True) rebuilds it from the cached collection without downloading, and a damaged selection is rebuilt rather than reported, since nothing in it is unrecoverable. Adding download_if_missing=True to that call lets it repair the source collection too, which does download.

docs.title: Use ORFdata with varcode, isovar, topiary and vaxrank
docs.text: Those tools read a PyEnsembl genome: a GTF of transcript models, plus transcript and protein FASTAs whose identifiers match the GTF. ORFdata writes exactly that for the two things a reference annotation leaves out — noncanonical ORFs and viral references — so a variant in either gets a coding consequence from the same tools that annotate reference transcripts.

docs.title: Three layers, three jobs
docs.text:
ORFdata keeps the molecular layers apart and names them the same way in every command and API:

Layer Molecule What it answers Who reads it genome DNA Where a read or a variant call sits Aligners; the contigs a VCF names transcriptome RNA What a variant does to a reading frame varcode, isovar proteome protein Which peptide a patient could present topiary, vaxrank, MS search

A DNA reference such as GDC's GRCh38.d1.vd1 is the genome layer: human chromosomes plus the viral sequences as extra contigs. It carries no transcript models and no proteins, which is what the other two layers supply.

docs.title: Viral transcripts in a tumour sample
docs.text:
Install the collection, or one cancer subset of it, and open it as a genome:

orfdata download viral --species human --subset cancer-causing
orfdata viral summary --subset cancer-causing

from varcode import Variant

from orfdata import select_viral_references, viral_genome

references = select_viral_references(
    subsets=["cancer-causing"], species="human", download_if_missing=True
)
genome = viral_genome(references)  # A PyEnsembl genome over the viral contigs.

variant = Variant(contig="AY446894.2", start=1500, ref="C", alt="T", genome=genome)
print(variant.effects().top_priority_effect().short_description)

viral_genome() indexes the set's annotation.gtf, transcripts.fasta and proteins.fasta into a PyEnsembl database kept beside the cache, never inside the checksummed reference directory. The same object goes to isovar with the tumour RNA alignment, and to topiary or vaxrank with an MHC predictor, wherever those take a genome.

Four things are worth knowing before the first run:

  • Contig names are the source accession.version, such as AY446894.2, because that is the record the sequences and the annotation come from. genomes.tsv keeps the inventory's source_genbank and source_refseq spellings beside it, so you can map the names your alignment used.
  • A non-standard genetic code is carried, as transl_table on the transcript and CDS rows, so PyEnsembl translates with the code the source record declares.
  • A partial or frameshifted source CDS gets no start or stop codon rows, so effect predictors will not translate it. annotation_complete says which transcripts are whole and partial says which end the source marks as running past the record: 78 of 1,703, mostly HPV E4 and E5 ORFs that are really expressed from spliced transcripts, plus HIV-1's pol, which is a Gag-Pol frameshift fusion. HPV16's E6, E7, E1, E2, L1 and L2 are complete, and HBV's polymerase is joined back together across the circular origin, so variants on either side of it get a coding consequence.
  • A coding transcript here is the CDS span, not a UTR-containing mRNA. The source records annotate 1,678 CDS features but only 39 mRNA features, so the transcriptome layer is built from the CDS features and says so rather than inventing transcript bounds.
