  • Three source records annotate no CDS at all — HPV2, HPV8 and HPV51 — so their coding features come from PaVE instead, on the identical sequence, and every transcript records which source annotated it. Use --no-annotation-fill to keep strictly to the GenBank submissions; orfdata viral summary then names the genomes that are left without transcripts. For the opposite trade — one source's uniform, spliced gene models everywhere it publishes the same molecule, in place of each submission's own naming — use --alternate-annotations, which leaves the genome FASTA byte-identical and adds 235 coding transcripts across the GDC collection. orfdata viral completeness shows what either choice leaves on the table.
  • A transcript's initiation says how the source starts it (atg, alternative, declared, non_canonical, partial, unknown) and recoding names any frameshift the source claims. Effect predictors handle a non-canonical start correctly, because the protein a source publishes is the one in proteins.fasta; they do not handle a variant at the base a ribosomal-frameshift join reads twice, which is two positions in HTLV-1.

docs.title: Noncanonical ORFs
docs.text:
Build a proteome as usual and ask for the matching annotation:

orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources ms \
  --output proteins.fasta --annotation ncorfs/

That writes ncorfs/annotation.gtf, ncorfs/transcripts.fasta and ncorfs/proteins.fasta: one coding transcript per ncORF, placed on its host gene, with the spliced coding sequence and the translation. In Python the same is proteome.write_annotation("ncorfs").

Catalogue imports preserve short translated ORFs for variant annotation. If a particular peptide-search workflow requires a length floor, add --min-protein-length 5; the generated proteome records the explicit policy and its omitted count, while the underlying catalogue remains complete.

from pyensembl import Genome

genome = Genome(
    reference_name="GRCh38",
    annotation_name="orfdata-ncorfs",
    annotation_version="1",
    gtf_path_or_url="ncorfs/annotation.gtf",
    transcript_fasta_paths_or_urls=["ncorfs/transcripts.fasta"],
    protein_fasta_paths_or_urls=["ncorfs/proteins.fasta"],
    cache_directory_path="ncorfs/index",
)
genome.index()

A variant inside an ncORF now has a protein consequence — a stop gained in a lncRNA ORF reads as p.K2* rather than disappearing into "non-coding transcript".

To keep the reference transcripts as well, concatenate the files instead of replacing them. PyEnsembl takes several FASTAs, and the ncORF GTF writes no gene rows precisely so it can be appended to an annotation that has them:

cat Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.115.gtf ncorfs/annotation.gtf > combined.gtf

genome = Genome(
    reference_name="GRCh38", annotation_name="ensembl-plus-ncorfs", annotation_version="115",
    gtf_path_or_url="combined.gtf",
    transcript_fasta_paths_or_urls=["Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.cdna.all.fa", "ncorfs/transcripts.fasta"],
    protein_fasta_paths_or_urls=["Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.pep.all.fa", "ncorfs/proteins.fasta"],
    cache_directory_path="combined/index",
)

For the models alone, without building a proteome, the query command writes the same GTF rows for any selection:

orfdata --evidence ms --format gtf > ncorfs.gtf
orfdata --gene LARP4B --format gtf

Two deliberate choices in that file:

  • ncORF transcripts are marked transcript_biotype "protein_coding", because each has a complete CDS with start and stop codons and effect predictors only translate transcripts marked that way. The source's own category stays in orf_biotype, and the host transcript in host_transcript_id.
  • The transcript is the ORF's coding path, so its identifier is the catalogue's orf_id. The protein is <orf_id>.p. Nothing is renamed to look like an Ensembl accession.

docs.title: What this does not claim
docs.text: An ORF model here is a catalogue ORF placed on an assembly, with the evidence the source reported; a predicted coding consequence is not evidence that a stable protein exists or that a peptide is presented. Viral collection and context membership record where a reference was selected, not that a virus drives a particular tumour. The layers stay separate so each of those questions can be asked of the right one.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Real cases from human Ensembl 115, from ordinary upstream ORFs to circular RNAs and processed precursors. The examples continue one Python session:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import ProteinProduct, SourceRNA, TranscriptORF, annotated_orfs, extra_orfs, rfam_ires

genome = EnsemblRelease(115, species="human")
orfs = extra_orfs(genome)  # Every bundled catalogue ORF on every transcript carrying it.

Coordinates are Python slices: transcript.sequence[orf.start:orf.end] is the coding sequence, including its stop codon, and protein products slice the protein sequence.

docs.title: ORF categories
docs.text:
Each catalogue ORF keeps its source category in orf_type. cds_relation is computed against the transcript's annotated CDS in the annotation you loaded:

examples = ["c10norep165", "c10norep53", "c10norep101", "c11riboseqorf10", "c11norep16", "c10norep110"]
for orf_id in examples:
    orf = orfs.for_orf(orf_id)[0]  # The transcript the source names comes first.
    print(orf.orf_type, orf.gene_name, orf.transcript_id, orf.start, orf.end, orf.cds_relation)

uORF FGFR2 ENST00000457416 96 198 upstream
uoORF EPC1 ENST00000375110 151 367 upstream_overlapping
intORF ANAPC16 ENST00000299381 296 365 internal
dORF TIMM10B ENST00000254616 929 1259 downstream
doORF PHLDA2 ENST00000314222 511 640 downstream_overlapping
lncRNA NUTM2B-AS1 ENST00000483080 88 199 no_cds

On their source transcripts in Ensembl 115, the two agree for over 98% of bundled ORFs:

orf_type (source) cds_relation (Ensembl 115) ORFs Other relations uORF upstream 2,972 11 uoORF upstream_overlapping 668 4 intORF internal 712 3 dORF downstream 487 11 doORF downstream_overlapping 60 1 lncRNA no_cds 1,892 4 processed_transcript no_cds 278 5

The exceptions mostly follow annotation changes since Ensembl 101, which the catalogue was built on. Keep both fields: the category is the source's, the relation describes the annotation you are using.

docs.title: Two proteins on one RNA
docs.text:
annotated_orfs(transcript) lists every annotated CDS a transcript carries, including other genes' proteins. MIURF's CDS lies in the "5′ UTR" of MIEF1's mRNA, and SNURF's in SNRPN's:

for transcript_id in ("ENST00000325301", "ENST00000390687"):  # MIEF1, SNRPN
    for orf in annotated_orfs(genome.transcript_by_id(transcript_id)):
        print(orf.gene_name, orf.source_gene_name, orf.orf_id, orf.start, orf.end, orf.cds_relation)

MIEF1 MIURF ENSP00000490747.1 176 389 upstream
MIEF1 MIEF1 ENSP00000390029.1 487 615 C_terminal_truncation
MIEF1 MIEF1 ENSP00000327124.2 487 1879 annotated_cds
SNRPN SNURF ENSP00000342152.4 62 278 upstream
SNRPN SNRPN ENSP00000462211.1 466 644 C_terminal_truncation
SNRPN SNRPN ENSP00000463510.1 466 974 C_terminal_truncation
SNRPN SNRPN ENSP00000375105.4 466 1189 annotated_cds

Each protein keeps its own ID and gene; gene_name is the RNA's gene. The C_terminal_truncation rows are shorter CDSs of other MIEF1 and SNRPN transcripts whose coding paths these RNAs also carry. Identical placements are reported once, with the other protein IDs in equivalent_ids.

docs.title: Starts other than AUG
docs.text:
Ensembl annotates some CDSs from CUG, GUG or AUU codons. Ensembl gives GUG and AUU starts no start_codon row; orfdata still reports them as complete, because the CDS begins inside its RNA:

for gene, transcript_id in (("EIF4G2", "ENST00000339995"), ("TEAD1", "ENST00000527636"), ("MYC", "ENST00000621592")):
    cds = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(genome.transcript_by_id(transcript_id))
    print(gene, cds.start_codon, cds.start_complete, cds.protein_sequence[:5], len(cds.protein_sequence))

EIF4G2 GTG True MESAI 907
TEAD1 ATT True MEPSS 426
MYC CTG True MDFFR 454

Isoforms initiated upstream of an annotated start can be read from the RNA with TranscriptORF.at. FGF2's annotated CDS starts at an AUG; UniProt P09038 documents CUG-initiated isoforms that extend it:

fgf2 = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000644866")
for start in (179, 221, 344):
    orf = TranscriptORF.at(fgf2, start, orf_id=f"FGF2@{start}", source="UniProt P09038")
    print(start, orf.start_codon, len(orf.protein_sequence), orf.end, orf.cds_relation)

179 CTG 210 812 N_terminal_extension
221 CTG 196 812 N_terminal_extension
344 ATG 155 812 annotated_cds

A start outside the genetic code's initiation codons must be declared, as in TranscriptORF.at(rna, start, start_codon="GTG", ...); otherwise the read is rejected. Catalogue models declare it with ORFModel(start_codon=...).

docs.title: Recoded stop codons and frameshifts
docs.text:
decoded_stop_codons lists internal stop codons that the protein reads through. GPX1 has a selenocysteine:

gpx1 = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000419783"))
print(gpx1.decoded_stop_codons)

((48, 'TGA', 'U'),)

Stop-codon readthrough can be described from its source. Eswarappa et al. (Cell 2014) report VEGFA's UGA stop decoded as serine, giving the 22-residue extension of VEGF-Ax:

vegfa = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000672860")
cds = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(vegfa)
ax = TranscriptORF.at(vegfa, cds.start, orf_id="VEGF-Ax", source="Eswarappa et al. 2014",
                      recoded={len(cds.protein_sequence): "S"})
print(ax.protein_sequence[len(cds.protein_sequence):], ax.cds_relation, ax.decoded_stop_codons)

SAGQEEGASLRVSGTRSLTRKD C_terminal_extension ((395, 'TGA', 'S'),)

Ensembl models programmed ribosomal frameshifts as one- or two-base gaps in the coding path. subcodon_introns reports them with the reading-frame shift:

oaz1 = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000602676"))
print(oaz1.subcodon_introns, len(oaz1.protein_sequence))

((204, 2271443, 2271443, 1),) 228

The skipped base is the T of the in-frame UGA after UCC, so antizyme 1 is read in the +1 frame from there. Some such gaps instead correct reference-sequence errors, so check the gene before interpreting one.

docs.title: Endogenous retrovirus proteins
docs.text:
Proteins from endogenous retroviruses that Ensembl annotates, such as syncytin-1 (ERVW-1) and syncytin-2 (ERVFRD-1), are part of the annotated proteome. Some catalogue ORFs have since become annotated proteins: the catalogue's lncRNA ORF c21norep46 is now ERVH48-1's CDS, which encodes suppressyn:

erv = orfs.for_orf("c21norep46")[0]
print(erv.orf_type, erv.gene_name, erv.cds_relation, len(erv.protein_sequence), erv.evidence.has_evidence("ms"))

lncRNA ERVH48-1 annotated_cds 160 True

Translated ERV sequences without an annotated transcript need genomic ORF models that orfdata does not yet support.

docs.title: Circular RNAs
docs.text:
SourceRNA represents an RNA that is not an annotated transcript, without inventing an Ensembl ID for it. circ-ZNF609 is ZNF609's second exon back-spliced into a circle (Legnini et al., Mol Cell 2017). Its ORF starts at the linear mRNA's AUG and reads across the junction:

znf609 = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000326648")
circ = SourceRNA.from_transcript(znf609, 261, 1135, id="circZNF609", source="Legnini et al. 2017",
                                 topology="circular")
orf = TranscriptORF.at(circ, 127, orf_id="circZNF609-ORF", source="Legnini et al. 2017")
print(len(circ.sequence), orf.segments, len(orf.coding_sequence), len(orf.protein_sequence), orf.coding_blocks)

874 ((127, 874), (0, 6)) 753 250 ((64499293, 64499298), (64499420, 64500166))

The 753-nt ORF crosses the junction and stops 6 bases after it, as the paper describes. The stop codon read after the junction is not in the linear mRNA, so the circular protein differs from ZNF609 after residue 249.

docs.title: Processed precursors
docs.text:
ProteinProduct slices a precursor's protein. POMC is cleaved into several hormones; positions here are from UniProt P01189 (entry version 239), whose 1-based ranges become Python slices. products_from_uniprot(entry) converts a whole UniProt JSON entry.

pomc = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000395826"))
products = [
    ProteinProduct("ACTH", "Corticotropin", "peptide", 137, 176, "UniProt P01189 v239"),
    ProteinProduct("alpha-MSH", "Melanotropin alpha", "peptide", 137, 150, "UniProt P01189 v239"),
    ProteinProduct("beta-endorphin", "Beta-endorphin", "peptide", 236, 267, "UniProt P01189 v239"),
]
for product in products:
    print(product.product_id, product.sequence(pomc)[:13], product.coding_slice(pomc), product.genomic_blocks(pomc))

ACTH SYSMEHFRWGKPV (514, 631) ((25161357, 25161473),)
alpha-MSH SYSMEHFRWGKPV (514, 553) ((25161435, 25161473),)
beta-endorphin YGGFMTSEKSQTP (811, 904) ((25161084, 25161176),)

coding_slice gives the product's codons in the transcript sequence and genomic_blocks their chromosome positions, so a variant in a precursor can be placed in each mature product.

docs.title: IRES elements
docs.text:
rfam_ires(rna) finds the human cellular internal ribosome entry site (IRES) sequences of Rfam 15.1 that occur exactly in an RNA:

for gene, transcript_id in (("MYC", "ENST00000621592"), ("VEGFA", "ENST00000672860"),
                            ("NTRK2", "ENST00000277120"), ("ODC1", "ENST00000234111")):
    transcript = genome.transcript_by_id(transcript_id)
    cds = TranscriptORF.from_annotation(transcript)
    for element in rfam_ires(transcript):
        print(gene, element.feature_id, element.start, element.end, "CDS starts", cds.start, cds.start_codon)

MYC RF00216:X00364.2/2502-2803 13 315 CDS starts 363 CTG
VEGFA RF00461:M63971.1/3107-3415 742 1051 CDS starts 496 CTG
NTRK2 RF00547:AF410902.1/3685-4037 179 532 CDS starts 532 ATG
ODC1 RF02535:AK292352.1/308-434 207 334 CDS starts 334 ATG

An IRES is an RNA feature, not an ORF category; an element can lie upstream of a CDS or inside it. The NTRK2 and ODC1 elements end exactly at the AUG, and the MYC element lies upstream of even the CUG-initiated CDS. The VEGFA element was defined upstream of the AUG-initiated protein, so it lies inside the longer CUG-initiated CDS that Ensembl annotates. The bundled families are those Rfam curates from published reports, and several cellular IRESs are disputed: dicistronic reporter assays can be confounded by cryptic promoters and splicing. A match locates a reported IRES sequence; it does not establish activity in that transcript or condition.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
For annotating a variant, look up the ORFs and features at its position:

print([(o.orf_id, o.transcript_id, o.cds_relation) for o in orfs.overlapping("7", 66205486, 66205486, genome_build="GRCh38")][:3])
myc_ires, = rfam_ires(genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000621592"))
print(myc_ires.genomic_blocks, myc_ires.overlaps("8", 127736300, 127736300))

[('c7riboseqorf56', 'ENST00000304842', 'upstream'), ('c7riboseqorf56', 'ENST00000904436', 'upstream'), ('c7riboseqorf56', 'ENST00000904438', 'upstream')]
((127736244, 127736545),) True

overlapping searches coding paths, optionally with initiation flanks; an RNA feature reports overlap through its genomic blocks.

docs.title: Matched human tissue RNA and protein abundance
docs.text:
The Wang et al. atlas measures adjacent cryosections from 29 healthy human tissue specimens. wang-human-tissue-abundance keeps six original table series in the same species-scoped API as dog, mouse and yeast data.

Source table Targets Native quantity EV1 protein groups 15,210 iBAQ EV1 genes 13,640 Author-normalized iBAQ EV2 transcripts 93,674 FPKM EV2 genes 18,072 Author-normalized FPKM EV5 protein groups 15,210 Estimated copies/cell EV5 transcripts 60,519 Estimated copies/cell

The download is approximately 397 MB and installs to a 3.86 GB SQLite database.

pip install 'orfdata'
orfdata datasets download wang-human-tissue-abundance --version 2026-10-12.1

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()
dataset = registry.open("wang-human-tissue-abundance", "2026-10-12.1")
reference, = dataset.manifest.references
gene = ScopedTarget(reference, "gene", "ENSG00000004059", "ensembl")  # ARF5
for value in dataset.measurements(target=gene, sample_id="V122"):
    print(value.quantity, value.value, value.unit, value.status)

Select the same gene on both sides for a specimen's native gene-level comparison:

match, = dataset.matched_measurements(
    allowed_bases=["adjacent_donor_tissue"],
    pair_ids=["rna_genes:protein_genes:V122"],
    left_target=gene, right_target=gene,
    left_filters={"unit": "FPKM"}, right_filters={"unit": "iBAQ"},
)
print(match.left[0].value, match.right[0].value)  # 51.09, 112559620.9

docs.title: Specimens and source cells
docs.text: There are 6,273,425 source cells. The same specimen has several processing views; these are not additional biological replicates. Native specimen IDs, RNA/MS run IDs, units, source cells and processing methods remain attached to the data. Bone marrow has no matched RNA column and is outside the 29-tissue dataset. Every source cell and RNA-copy input link was independently reconciled before publication. Missing or censored cells remain explicit observations.

docs.title: PyEnsembl targets and search references
docs.text: With Ensembl 83 already installed in PyEnsembl, the same target can be built with ScopedTarget.from_pyensembl(gene_object, kind="gene", namespace="ensembl", context=reference). The context pins the historical GRCh38.p5 assembly accession, GTF and complete Ensembl 83 protein FASTA. Alternate-reference protein entries absent from the GTF remain in the native search set. Search lookups preserve versioned FASTA IDs; they do not silently strip versions or imply detection.

docs.title: Interpreting the values
docs.text:
Protein-group values remain group observations. Representative proteins and their parent genes/transcripts are context, with unresolved individual attribution. The source's gene-level summaries permit gene-level RNA/protein comparisons; they do not quantify a particular isoform, uORF or ncORF. Pairings explicitly use adjacent_donor_tissue, independently of the target relationship. See the comparison API for selecting pairings and deriving ratios.

Protein copies are the authors' proteomic-ruler estimates, not isotope-standard measurements. Raw intensity inputs and per-sample calibration constants are absent from these tables; corresponding iBAQ observations are linked as associated data, not falsely recorded as the ruler's inputs. RNA copies link their source FPKM cells and retain the assumption that mRNA constitutes 2% of total RNA mass. Unreported calibration uncertainty stays unknown.

Protein zeros are unquantified values; gene-RNA and transcript-copy zeros retain the source censoring semantics. They are not measurements of biological absence. The methods state a 1-FPKM threshold, but gene values undergo median normalization; 2,677 positive gene values are below 1. Their values remain intact, and no numeric detection limit is invented in normalized units. Unfiltered transcript FPKM retains its native zeros and tiny numeric text values; a nonzero estimate does not establish expression above the study's 1-FPKM cutoff. Original numeric text and zero sentinels remain in provenance. Stable identifiers join the source tables even when their display gene labels differ.

docs.title: Related reanalysis and terms
docs.text:
The Eraslan reanalysis selects major isoforms and normalizes exon/intron counts differently. It is a separate planned view of the same specimens, not silently mixed into this release. These tables cover canonical coding-gene expression; they add RNA/protein context without expanding the experimental noncanonical-ORF catalogue.

Source supplements retain CC-BY-4.0 attribution, and Ensembl annotations retain their source terms. Discovery and installed queries work offline; acquisition and source rebuilding are explicit through DataCache.

docs.title: Yeast RNA and ribosome occupancy
docs.text:
ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo contains the processed RNA and ribosome-footprint measurements from Ingolia et al. (2009), GSE13750. It uses the same dataset API as human, mouse and dog.

pip install 'orfdata'
orfdata datasets info ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo
orfdata datasets download ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo

The download is about 24 MB compressed, 210 MB installed. It contains 329,952 observations: counts, reads/kb and RPKM for 13,748 source regions in eight libraries. Four libraries measure RNA and four measure ribosome footprints, in rich medium or after 20 minutes of amino-acid starvation. Source sample titles identify the modality, condition and nominal replicate. In particular, GSM346114 is Footprints-rich-2 despite its fp_rich1 filename.

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

dataset = DatasetRegistry().open("ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo")
reference, = dataset.manifest.references
target = ScopedTarget(reference, "region", "HRA1", "Ingolia2009:feature")
for measurement in dataset.measurements(target=target, unit="RPKM"):
    print(measurement.sample_id, measurement.quantity, measurement.value)

Queries work offline after download. quantity="rna_abundance" or quantity="ribosome_occupancy" selects one modality. unit="counts" returns the original aligned read counts. The other two native series have origin="derived" and link to their count observation. Source formulas, feature lengths and total CDS-aligned reads remain attached; the reported rounded values are preserved. Zeros remain measured zeros. GSM346118 has no zero-count rows; ORFdata does not add or remove a pseudocount.

docs.title: What these regions establish
docs.text:
The source includes 3,523 5′ UTRs, 4,592 3′ UTRs, 225 intron windows and 5,408 other feature labels, including coding, ncRNA and mitochondrial labels. Ribosome occupancy over a UTR does not identify a particular uORF. These targets therefore retain kind="region"; they do not expand the experimental ORF catalogue or establish stable protein abundance, copies/cell or translation flux.

The yeast reference has taxon 4932 and the source annotation date, SGD 2008-06-22. Exact genomic windows and assembly remain unresolved, including the UTR definitions attributed to Nagalakshmi et al. (2008). The biological strain BY4741 is sample metadata. Current PyEnsembl coordinates cannot be substituted for these historical windows without a validated mapping.

The paper reports RNA and footprints from the same samples, but the exact GSM-to-GSM aliquot crosswalk is unresolved. The release retains eight separate libraries and creates no assay pairs or translation-efficiency ratios. It also does not pair these cultures with the separate CoPY protein study. Issue #11 tracks these source gaps.

To rebuild, install orfdata and run orfdata datasets build ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo, or DatasetRegistry().build("ingolia-yeast-rna-ribo"). All 17 source inputs have pinned URLs, sizes and checksums. Verified local inputs can be supplied through --source-path ASSET=PATH or source_paths={...}. Query a local build using DatasetRegistry().open_build(...) or orfdata datasets query ... --built.

docs.title: Paired canine mammary-stroma RNA and protein
docs.text:
canine-mammary-stroma imports the processed measurements of Amini et al. (2021), GSE135183 and PXD023023. It uses the same data commands and QuantitativeDataset API as other species and sources:

orfdata data info canine-mammary-stroma
orfdata data fetch canine-mammary-stroma
orfdata data path canine-mammary-stroma

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry

registry = DatasetRegistry()
dataset = registry.open("canine-mammary-stroma")  # Offline; no implicit download.
rna_reference, protein_reference = dataset.manifest.references
pairs = list(dataset.pairings())
complete_pairs = [pair for pair in pairs if pair.right_assay_id is not None]
pair = complete_pairs[0]
rna = dataset.measurements(
    reference=pair.reference, assay_id=pair.left_assay_id, unit="estimated_count"
)
protein = dataset.measurements(
    reference=pair.right_reference, assay_id=pair.right_assay_id, unit="LFQ intensity"
)

The release contains 993,560 native measurements in a 52 MB download and a 514 MB installed SQLite file. Rebuilding uses approximately 8 MB of pinned processed inputs; no raw MS files, sequencing reads, alignment index or vendor database is required.

Layer Native scope Quantities RNA 18,582 Ensembl gene IDs × 30 samples, 15 cases Integer estimated counts from Kallisto/tximport Protein 1,583 native MaxQuant groups × 28 samples, 14 cases Intensity, LFQ intensity, iBAQ Peptide 5,413 native peptide rows × 28 samples Intensity and the separately reported LFQ intensity columns

Different quantitative columns do not add biological replicates. The 58 assays retain their original sample and run identities. Native MS rows include 77 reversed protein groups and 52 contaminant groups; these counts are not counts of confidently detected canine proteins.

docs.title: Specimen pairing
docs.text:
The authors reused archived FFPE mammary specimens for separate laser-capture RNA and protein preparations. The importer verifies a unique match between clinical Table 1 and GEO by breed, age and histological subtype, recording spelling normalizations and both original sets of labels. This is a metadata-derived crosswalk within an author-declared shared cohort, not an author-provided case-ID mapping.

Fourteen shared cases give 28 complete assay pairs: normal stroma and cancer-associated stroma separately. Two RNA samples from GEO case 127 have explicitly missing protein mates; the paper reports exclusion of proteomics case 7 because its paraffin block was unavailable. No protein sample is invented.

These pairs use same_specimen. This basis means separate preparations from the same original specimen, without claiming identical aliquots or adjacent sections. Temporal labels refer to the original biological specimen, not the dates of RNA sequencing and mass-spectrometry acquisition. Missing mates retain an unknown temporal relationship. Pairing does not itself establish a relationship between RNA genes and protein groups: this release has no cross-modal target relations or current-reference mappings.

The normal compartment belongs to a cancer-bearing mammary specimen. It is not a healthy-animal normal-tissue atlas. Source case IDs identify individual specimens, and repeated compartments or quantities never imply additional dogs.

docs.title: Missingness, native records and reference limits
docs.text:
• RNA zeros remain measured zero counts. Counts are estimated gene-level values, with no conversion to TPM, copies per cell or translation efficiency.
  • MaxQuant MS zeros denote unquantified cells. Their numeric values are None with status missing; the original "0" survives in provenance. The 2,156 native "NaN" iBAQ cells also remain missing, with a separate reason.
  • Every native MS field survives once in the corresponding mapping's provenance["native_record"]. Measurements retain source row/column, original numeric text, identification type and the original control/decoy flags.
  • Peptide mappings retain every reported native protein-group ID. A unique assignment to one group is not unique protein or isoform detection. Group records retain reported protein labels, including contaminants, without assigning them to a canine biological protein reference.
  • No source QC threshold, aggregation, imputation, differential-expression model or RNA/protein ratio is applied. Consumers can inspect the native flags and scores explicitly.

RNA was quantified against Ensembl transcripts on CanFam3.1; its exact release and transcript sequence bytes are not reported. The protein search used a canonical UniProt dog reference dated 2019-07-29 with decoys and contaminants; the searched FASTA is absent from the deposited processed files. Both references remain source-bound and incomplete. Source membership and uniqueness flags are preserved, but no full-background sequence uniqueness is asserted. These data provide neither ncORF translation evidence nor MHC-presentation evidence.

The earlier source audit records the acquisition and crosswalk evidence. The PRIDE project declares CC0; GEO numerical data and factual metadata use GEO's public-data terms. Factual clinical curation cites Table 1 of the CC BY-NC-ND article. Its original text and figures are excluded from the dataset artifact.

docs.title: RNA, ribosome and protein measurements
docs.text:
The quantitative layer of orfdata stores measurements of genes, transcripts, reference ORFs, proteins, protein groups, peptides and source-defined regions. A measurement stays at the resolution the experiment supports. Parent-gene RNA abundance is useful context for an ORF; it is not a separate measurement of each ORF in that gene.

Released datasets, each with its own guide:

  • Human, mouse and dog protein abundance (Pfizer/Oziolor atlas)
  • Dog and mouse RNA abundance (Pfizer/Oziolor atlas)
  • Matched human tissue RNA and protein (Wang et al.)
  • Yeast protein and RNA abundance (CoPY)
  • Yeast RNA and ribosome occupancy (Ingolia et al.)
  • Dog MHC ligands and PeptideAtlas peptides (Kaabinejadian et al.; Kusebauch et al.)
  • Pfizer dog peptide and protein-group evidence (Oziolor et al.)

See released coverage and gaps; the data roadmap tracks further imports. The bundled human ORF evidence catalogue remains available offline. Its pooled PSM counts describe spectra, not sample-level protein abundance.

docs.title: Discover, download and query
docs.text:
Install orfdata to manage datasets. Creating a registry and listing releases reads metadata only:

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()  # Metadata only; no download.
releases = registry.list(species="dog", assay="digest_ms")

For a registered release:

Call What it does registry.info(name, version) Returns its immutable manifest. registry.download(name, version) Fetches and verifies it. registry.open(name, version) Reads it offline. registry.inspect(name, version) Reports missing, available or invalid files without downloading or repairing them. registry.download_metadata(name, version) Returns the artifact's access terms and file hashes and sizes.

An invalid cache requires an explicit download(..., force=True); old reader paths survive. Python download options such as timeout, retries and progress go to DataCache.

Query an opened dataset by an exact, reference-scoped target. Here transcript is a PyEnsembl Transcript in the dataset's exact reference context:

dataset = registry.open(name, version)
target = ScopedTarget.from_pyensembl(
    transcript, kind="transcript", namespace="ensembl:110"
)
for measurement in dataset.measurements(target=target):
    print(measurement.value, measurement.unit, measurement.status)

Use ScopedTarget.from_orf(bound_reference_orf, namespace=source_release) for a validated reference ORF. Namespaces and identifiers must match the source's mapping table. The default PyEnsembl target uses its unversioned id; request versioned=True when the source uses versioned identifiers. There is no implicit mapping across annotation releases, gene isoforms, ORFs or species. A variant or fusion product does not inherit a native reference protein measurement.

Use ScopedTarget(reference, "region", source_id, source_namespace) for a quantified UTR, intron or other source-defined window. Keep its native feature type and target length in measurement provenance. A region ID does not assert known genomic coordinates or a translated ORF. RNA and Ribo measurements of the same region can be compared through an explicit same_target relationship; such a density ratio describes that region, not a particular uORF inside it. Regions do not automatically bind to PyEnsembl or participate in gene/ORF orthology.

When a source also defines a candidate or partial coding model, connect the two with TargetRelation(..., relation="region_orf_context", ...): the left target is the measured region; the right is an orf target created from its TranscriptORF with ScopedTarget.from_orf. Annotated and source-defined ORFs work without a catalogue record. Supply the source's mapping evidence, such as the reported interval relationship, coordinates and source record IDs, and its cardinality (one_to_many or unknown when appropriate). Keep each candidate as its own relation. This preserves a region's relationship to coding models without converting region measurements into ORF abundance or translation evidence. MatchedMeasurements.ratio rejects this context relation even if the source reports only one candidate. Partial boundary/frame details remain on the referenced ORF; the relation does not fill them in.

For native sources with unreported genomic metadata, use explicit source references and mapping views to retain the original observation alongside its mapping to a PyEnsembl target.

Choose a native series explicitly when a source supplies several units:

values = dataset.measurements(quantity="protein_abundance", unit="iBAQ", scale="linear")
dataset.export_parquet("ibaq.parquet", unit="iBAQ", scale="linear")

unit, scale and log_base also work with mapped_measurements and existing storage v1-v4 releases. Units are exact and case-sensitive. Selecting scale="log", log_base=2 returns values already on that scale; nothing is transformed. An unavailable series returns no observations. Contradictory linear/log requests raise an error. Omitting selectors preserves all native series.

For example, Pfizer iBAQ and rIBAQ are two series from the same source rows. Selecting or exporting both does not create additional donors, spectra or independent detections. Source row/sample/assay lineage stays attached to each measurement.

The CLI uses the same operations:

orfdata datasets list --species yeast
orfdata datasets info DATASET --version RELEASE
orfdata datasets download DATASET --version RELEASE
orfdata datasets inspect DATASET --version RELEASE
orfdata datasets query DATASET --version RELEASE --quantity protein_abundance

Queries stream JSON lines. --reference ref:SHA256 selects an exact context; target queries also require --target, --kind and --namespace. Unqualified sample/assay ID queries across multiple references are rejected. Existing catalogue commands such as orfdata --gene TPST1 retain their behavior.

docs.title: What each value means
docs.text:
Measurement retains the dataset/version, reference-scoped target, sample and assay IDs, value, native unit, linear/log scale and log base, uncertainty and its definition, detection limit, status, origin and provenance. Measured zero, below detection, not measured, not mapped and missing are distinct. Censored or missing values use None; native sentinels can remain in provenance.

RNA counts/TPM/FPKM, ribosome occupancy, source-defined translation efficiency, LFQ/iBAQ/TMT values, peptide intensity, PSM counts, copies per cell and turnover remain distinct. No conversion is automatic. Derived/predicted values name a method and retain source/input provenance. An estimate from calibration remains an estimate; an intensity/TPM ratio does not acquire molecule-ratio units.

Sample records biological units, pools and source labels. Assay separately records technical replicates, runs, fractions, TMT plex/channel/bridge, normalization and calibration. A sample's strain/breed belongs in its attributes; it need not be the strain used to assemble its reference genome. TargetMapping retains all candidate assignments, an unmapped reason, or known candidates with an explicit unresolved reason when source endpoints are missing. A protein-group representative does not become a uniquely measured protein. See pairing and orthology comparisons for explicit experimental relationships and derived RNA/protein ratios.

The public query shapes are shared across sources and species: samples(), assays(), measurements(), mappings(), relations() and reference_mappings(). Source-specific fields stay in evidence and provenance; native-table inspection belongs in the source modules. For example:

assignments = dataset.mappings(source_identifier=peptide_sequence)
for assignment in assignments:
    print(assignment.status, assignment.targets, assignment.method)

mappings() also accepts an exact source_namespace, reference or destination target. Selecting one destination preserves all candidates in each returned mapping. Reported assignments and computed sequence compatibility remain separate records with explicit methods and evidence. Mapping status describes the assignment's cardinality or completeness, not independent protein detection.

docs.title: Importing a source
docs.text:
Define a DatasetManifest with exact reference contexts, raw source URLs, SHA-256 hashes and byte sizes, citations, file-specific access/redistribution terms, searched/measurable coverage, processing software/version/parameters and row accounting. Unavailable metadata stay unknown. Article licensing does not substitute for the data files' terms.

An importer calls QuantitativeDataset.create(path, manifest, samples=..., assays=..., measurements=..., mappings=...). These inputs may be generators; measurements are written incrementally.

Every observation names a source asset or earlier input measurements. Derived inputs precede outputs in the same dataset release. A derived measurement names its inputs in one of two forms, which cannot be mixed:

  • input_measurements: IDs within the output reference.
  • input_references: MeasurementReference records with each input's dataset, version, reference and ID.

Cross-species derived abundance is rejected. Duplicate IDs, broken foreign keys, wrong dataset releases and cross-reference links fail the import. Failed builds do not replace data.

Use build_dataset(manifest, builder, ...) for a managed local import. builder(source_paths, output_path) reads the verified inputs and creates that SQLite dataset. DataCache publishes it atomically with input/output checksums and a processing receipt. source_paths={asset_id: local_file} supports manually acquired sources. Importing locally does not grant redistribution rights.

A DatasetRegistry(definitions, cache_root=...) registers releases as:

definitions = {
    name: {
        "default_version": version,
        "versions": {version: {
            "manifest": manifest.to_dict(),
            "distribution": {"access_terms": terms, "redistributable": False},
            "assets": {"dataset.sqlite": {
                "url": url, "sha256": sha256, "size": size, "decompress": False,
            }},
        }},
    }
}

CLI users can supply this JSON with orfdata datasets --registry FILE ....

docs.title: Rebuilding a release from source
docs.text:
Rebuild supported releases from their pinned original inputs with registry.build(name, version, source_paths={"asset_id": "/local/file"}) or orfdata datasets build NAME --source-path ASSET=PATH. Local overrides still require the published hashes. Rebuilds use a separate import cache and preserve installed releases. Unsupported source importers fail explicitly.

Use registry.open_build(name, version) to reopen a source rebuild offline, or registry.inspect_build(name, version) to inspect it. Normal open still selects the published artifact. The CLI makes the same choice explicit:

orfdata datasets build DATASET --version RELEASE
orfdata datasets inspect DATASET --version RELEASE --built
orfdata datasets query DATASET --version RELEASE --built --unit counts

pairs --built also uses the local rebuild. Read operations never acquire or repair data.

Build inspection checks source pins, transform identity and output bytes against the saved receipt, even after local source overrides have been removed. Its verified field remains false because a build receipt is not an independent published output checksum. Both cache origins retain their original paths and provenance; explicit force rebuilding preserves existing readers.

docs.title: Cache location and storage
docs.text:
The cache root is ORFDATA_CACHE, then OPENVAX_DATA_CACHE, then the platform's OpenVax cache. orfdata owns its orfdata/ child. Release cache identities include manifest/reference and content hashes.

Datasets are SQLite files. Every table is partitioned by reference key, with composite foreign keys, so human, mouse, dog, yeast and arbitrary other taxa use the same schema. Compact storage and compatibility describes new SQLite v4 writes, legacy readers and actual-source size/query benchmarks.

The normal installation includes pandas and PyArrow. Use dataset.export_parquet(path) to export query columns alongside the full measurement JSON, preserving exact values and provenance even when a floating-point analysis column cannot represent an integer exactly.

docs.title: Comparing RNA, ribosome and protein abundance
docs.text:
Use declared experimental relationships to compare assays. A tissue label alone does not make an RNA sample and a protein sample a matched pair.

for match in dataset.matched_measurements(allowed_bases=["same_material"]):
    row = match.to_table_row()
    print(row["rna_abundance"], row["protein_abundance"])

Rows include named RNA, ribosome occupancy, translation-efficiency, protein, peptide and spectrum-count columns, each containing original measurement records with units, missingness and provenance. Missing columns are empty lists. Multiple values remain multiple values; the API does not average them or create a Cartesian product of technical replicates. Each row retains its assay pairing and target relationship. A three-assay experiment can declare several pairwise comparisons; sharing an RNA measurement does not create independent replicates.

Pairing bases are same_material, same_specimen, adjacent_donor_tissue, biological_replicate, independent_cultures, tissue_aggregate and condition_aggregate. The caller must choose the allowed bases. By default, only explicitly concurrent assays are returned; opt into longitudinal or unknown with allowed_temporal. Missing mates stay explicit. Technical runs, TMT channels and bridges remain in the assays and do not become biological sample counts.

RNA annotation and protein search references can differ. AssayPair.reference is the left assay's context; right_reference explicitly identifies the right assay's context and defaults to the left for older records. Both must belong to the same species. A protein FASTA does not need an invented genomic assembly: see source references. Original targets and references remain attached to both sides, even when their local IDs happen to match.

The CLI streams the same table rows:

orfdata datasets pairs DATASET --version RELEASE --basis same_material

Select exact targets with left_target=... and right_target=..., using the same ScopedTarget objects as ordinary measurement queries, including targets constructed from PyEnsembl genes. reference identifies the left context; a left target supplies that scope when omitted. Each right target keeps its own native reference. Incompatible species or reference selections fail explicitly.

left_filters and right_filters select native quantity, status, unit, scale and log_base. They do not override assay identities. Pairing strength and target attribution are unchanged; filtered-out values leave empty sides, not measured zeros.

pair_ids and relation_ids select original source IDs. Relationships can also be inspected with dataset.relations(left_target=gene) or dataset.pairings(pair_ids=[...], reference=reference) without scanning unrelated Python objects. See the human example.

CLI equivalents use --left-unit, --right-unit and the other prefixed native filters. A target requires all four of --left-target, --left-kind, --left-namespace and --left-reference (or the corresponding --right-... arguments). ID selectors remain --pair-id and --relation-id.

docs.title: Which targets are being compared?
docs.text:
TargetRelation links exact, reference-scoped targets with mapping evidence and cardinality. same_target compares one target across assays/samples. canonical_translation links a gene/transcript to its annotated protein. parent_rna_context links parent RNA to an ORF but keeps the RNA value attached to its original gene/transcript. shared_group_member records an ambiguous protein-group assignment; the group value stays a group value. gene_protein_group_context links RNA to an ambiguous source protein group without assigning that group's abundance to an individual protein or ORF.

Importers pass AssayPair and TargetRelation iterators as pairings= and relations= to QuantitativeDataset.create. IDs belong to the dataset release and left reference context. The right assay/target keeps its own context. Invalid assay references, contradictory known donor identities and conflicting one-to-one assignments fail the import. Original storage-version-1 datasets remain readable and have no declared relationships.

docs.title: Ratios are derived measurements
docs.text:
ratio = match.ratio(
    selected_protein_measurement, selected_rna_measurement,
    measurement_id="ratio-1", method="native protein/RNA ratio",
    normalization={"protein": "source bridge normalization", "rna": "source TPM"},
)

Select actual measurements from opposite sides of the match. Ratios require one-to-one target attribution and linear inputs. Parent-RNA/ORF and shared-group links cannot produce target-specific ratios. There is no implicit log conversion, unit conversion, replicate averaging or uncertainty propagation.

An iBAQ/TPM ratio keeps (iBAQ)/(TPM) units. Copies-per-cell values also retain their native composite units and the calibration recorded on their source assays. Missing, censored or nonpositive denominators produce an unresolved not_measured result with its reason, never infinity or a measured zero. RPF/RNA ratios are source-defined translation-efficiency measures, not measured flux. All derived values retain their input IDs, pairing, target attribution and normalization assumptions. When input reference contexts differ, the ratio stores MeasurementReference records in input_references, rather than unqualified local IDs. This preserves source identity across annotation and search-FASTA releases.

docs.title: Across species
docs.text:
compare_orthologs(left_dataset, right_dataset, mappings) is separate and opt-in. Each OrthologyMapping pins its source file, release, both reference contexts, cardinality, confidence definition and evidence. The default accepts one-to-one canonical gene mappings; one-to-many relationships require explicit permission through allowed_cardinalities.

The result contains each species' original observations. It neither merges identities nor transfers abundance or protein-existence evidence. ORF comparisons additionally require their own sequence, frame and positional evidence and allow_orfs=True; a gene ortholog cannot establish an orthologous ncORF. Human, mouse, dog, yeast and arbitrary other taxa use this same API.

same_specimen records separate preparations from the same original specimen. It does not assert identical aliquots (same_material) or adjacent sections. The canine mammary-stroma dataset uses this distinction and retains missing mates explicitly.

docs.title: Pfizer dog peptide and protein-group evidence
docs.text:
pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence adds the underlying peptide, PSM, protein-group and reporter evidence from the Oziolor et al. atlas, MassIVE MSV000099744 / PXD070290. Its companion pfizer-atlas-dog-protein retains the published iBAQ/rIBAQ summary. They describe the same experiment.

Release 2026-10-27.1, available with ORFdata 0.40.0 or later, downloads 6.90 GB in 4 compressed parts and installs a 24.71 GB SQLite artifact. The full build and native-source acceptance receipts are included in the data release.

docs.title: Coverage and interpretation
docs.text:
The selected source contains 70,280,798 records across 42 tables, including 49,192,521 reported membership links. It retains target and decoy partitions, confidence definitions, modifications, acquisition identifiers and quantitative vectors. Spectral peak arrays, chromatograms and workflow/UI payloads are excluded. The source lineage covers 96 runs and 44 channels: 38 tissue pools, four bridges and two empty channels. A positive pool does not identify individual positive dogs.

The deposited FASTA has 20,649 searched sequences. The independent sequence audit found 953,980 distinct target peptide sequences and 1,171,840 compatible placements: 1,132,603 exact and 39,237 additional isoleucine/leucine-equivalent placements. Reported source memberships and sequence-compatible candidates are separate queries. A candidate placement does not establish unique protein attribution. The FASTA excludes spliced isoforms; it is not a complete canine isoform background.

No confidence threshold or new normalization is applied. Native confidence, exclusion, modification and ambiguity fields remain available for an explicit downstream policy. Decoy records remain controls even when their native confidence label is high. Bulk tissue MS supplies no normal-tissue DLA-presentation evidence and does not add noncanonical ORFs to the dog proteome.

docs.title: Explicit download and offline queries
docs.text:
orfdata datasets download pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence

The download installs a checksummed SQLite artifact from ordered compressed parts. Normal imports and queries do not acquire the 86 GB vendor database or a separate source FASTA. After installation:

from itertools import islice
from orfdata import DatasetRegistry

dataset = DatasetRegistry().open("pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence")
target = next(dataset.measurements(status="measured")).target

for value in islice(dataset.measurements(target=target), 10):
    print(value.sample_id, value.assay_id, value.unit, value.value, value.status)

# The same TargetMapping model used by other peptide datasets.
assignments = list(dataset.mappings(reference=target.reference,
                                   source_identifier=target.identifier))
for assignment in assignments:
    print(assignment.evidence["basis"], assignment.status, assignment.targets)

# The same TargetRelation model used for other group memberships.
protein = next(t for assignment in assignments for t in assignment.targets)
groups = list(dataset.relations(right_target=protein))

These are the same high-level queries and return types used for other sources and species. A reported assignment is tied to its original peptide-group or PSM record; a sequence_compatibility mapping retains all compatible proteins and positions separately. Selecting one destination with mappings(target=protein) still returns every candidate in each selected mapping. An incomplete reported assignment has status unresolved, a reason and any known candidates. A unique mapping does not independently establish protein detection.

Measurement units name the original column: PD2.4 TargetPeptideGroups.Abundances, PD2.4 TargetPeptideGroups.AbundancesNormalized, PD2.4 TargetPeptideGroups.AbundancesScaled or PD2.4 TargetPsms.Abundances. These are distinct series, not calibrated copies per cell or the summary's iBAQ. Numeric zeros remain measured zeros. Null and nonfinite values remain explicitly missing, with their native state preserved in provenance. The low-level adapter’s missing_acquisitions() reports requested acquisition keys with no source row, which differs from a present row with missing quantities. Queries stream observations from compact vectors rather than loading a dense matrix.

Group relations retain the pinned same-study protein-summary context. They neither transfer a group's abundance to an individual protein nor supply another independent measurement. Publication and deposit instrument reports remain explicit where unresolved.

For low-level inspection of vendor table IDs, decoy controls, confidence definitions or individual acquisition records, use the source adapter explicitly:

from orfdata.sources.pfizer_attribution import CanineEvidence

native = CanineEvidence(dataset.path)
context = native.summary_group("A0A5F4CET6")

This adapter exposes native records without changing the source-independent measurement, mapping and relationship APIs.

docs.title: Reproducibility and source integrity
docs.text:
The published source component retains every selected typed value. Full-source acceptance compares the consumer artifact against the native export, checks membership endpoints and quantitative axes, and verifies the independently established candidate digest. Source and artifact archives retain separate hashes for compressed parts and their installed logical file.

Rebuilding from the pinned normalized sources is explicit:

dataset = DatasetRegistry().build("pfizer-atlas-dog-peptide-evidence")

The returned dataset uses the same query API. Use open_build() to reopen a local rebuild, whose own output checksum is recorded in its build receipt.

The builder creates one private database and publishes it only after complete integrity checks. With the 32 GiB output cap, an already expanded source requires 34.4 GB of additional free space; this is a safety reservation, not the measured artifact size. This release measured 24.71 GB of additional build files at peak. Compressed source acquisition also needs space for its expansion. Interrupted builds remove their own private output and preserve existing datasets. See the extraction and build guide for the selected tables, resource receipts and provenance.

Selective FTPS acquisition checked remote identity, offsets, lengths and acquired chunk hashes. There is no authoritative checksum for the entire vendor database; the recorded integrity claim covers the selected acquired facts. Source records are CC0 under the MassIVE deposit, and searched FASTA records retain UniProt attribution and CC-BY-4.0 terms. Compiled lineage retains factual source locations; the publication's original supplementary workbook is not redistributed.

docs.title: Human, mouse and dog protein abundance
docs.text:
The Oziolor et al. atlas provides parallel TMT protein measurements. ORFdata keeps each species in a separate dataset, using the same samples, assays, measurements and query API.

The dog peptide and protein-group evidence extension adds native memberships and peptide/PSM quantities while retaining this summary as same-study context.

Dataset Reported protein groups Source channels Source rows pfizer-atlas-human-protein 10,352 37 325,702 pfizer-atlas-mouse-protein 12,124 63 615,991 pfizer-atlas-dog-protein 9,929 38 313,263

Release 2026-10-12.1 contains the complete March 23, 2026 summary tables from MassIVE MSV000099729, MSV000099754 and MSV000099744, respectively. Each source row contributes two observations: native iBAQ and rIBAQ. Neither is calibrated copies per cell. These are pooled tissue samples; rodent condition labels also include sex. Channels and technical runs do not count as independent donors.

pip install 'orfdata'
orfdata datasets list --species dog
orfdata datasets download pfizer-atlas-dog-protein
orfdata datasets query pfizer-atlas-dog-protein --quantity protein_abundance --unit iBAQ --scale linear

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()
dataset = registry.open("pfizer-atlas-dog-protein")  # After explicit download.
reference, = dataset.manifest.references
group = ScopedTarget(reference, "protein_group", "A0A0A0MPB0", "MSV000099744:ProteinGroup")
for value in dataset.measurements(target=group, unit="iBAQ", scale="linear"):
    print(value.sample_id, value.unit, value.value, value.status)

Omit the unit selector to return both native series. They retain the same source row and sample identity; two units do not imply two independent measurements.

Every target retains its species and the checksum of the deposited UniProt search FASTA. The original genomic assembly and UniProt release are unknown. They stay unknown; a future annotation mapping must be explicit and validated. Group representatives can be inspected through reference_mappings(), but their lookup does not establish all group members. Opting into unresolved mapped views keeps the original group measurement visible, without assigning its value to an individual protein. No RNA pairings are inferred in this release.

The complete search references are available through registry.download_reference(name) and registry.open_reference(name) without rebuilding abundance. This includes proteins without reported representatives; search membership is separate from detection or protein-group assignment.

Source NA values remain missing and numeric zeros remain measured zeros. Absent group/channel combinations have no observation. For dog, 64,039 combinations are absent and eight reported rows contain NA, reproducing the existing 64,047 missing iBAQ matrix cells. Each value retains its source line, column, original numeric text, representative, normalization sum and native Abundance field. Nonfinite transformed strings such as -Inf are kept as provenance only.

These searches used UniProt sequences without spliced isoforms. Coverage does not establish that an unreported ncORF was searched or absent, nor does bulk tissue MS establish MHC presentation. The article and deposit disagree on the instrument name; that discrepancy remains explicit in assay metadata.

Downloads are 87.3 MB (human), 154.8 MB (mouse) and 84.4 MB (dog). Installed SQLite files occupy 1.46 GB, 2.72 GB and 1.40 GB, respectively. Queries stream observations; they do not load the entire file or a dense matrix into memory.

Source tables are CC0 according to the MassIVE deposits; UniProt search records retain UniProt Consortium attribution and CC-BY-4.0 terms. Both sources have pinned hashes and sizes. The data artifact is separate from the Python package. Discovery and installed queries work offline. download verifies and installs the compressed artifact; it does not fetch the large vendor search database.

To reproduce a source import, use registry.build(name, source_paths=...), orfdata datasets build NAME, or orfdata.sources.pfizer.build_protein("dog"). The source overrides are protein.tsv and search.fasta; DataCache verifies their original checksums before running the importer. Source slices with actual positive, zero and missing values test the same importer for all three species.

docs.title: Dog and mouse RNA abundance
docs.text:
The Oziolor et al. atlas deposits native gene counts alongside its protein measurements. ORFdata preserves each species separately, using the same measurement API.

Dataset RNA libraries Measured genes Observations Reference pfizer-atlas-dog-rna 434 30,941 13,428,394 ROS_Cfam_1.0, Ensembl 110 pfizer-atlas-mouse-rna 606 56,051 33,966,906 GRCm39, Ensembl 110

The dog download is about 534 MB and installs to 3.41 GB; the mouse download is 1.27 GB and installs to 8.66 GB. Queries select observations from the installed SQLite database without loading the whole matrix into memory.

The original rcnt values are integer gene counts after the authors' modified nf-core/Salmon pipeline. They are neither TPM nor calibrated RNA copies per cell. Zeros stay measured zeros: 4,218,202 dog observations and 18,019,555 mouse observations. Every value retains the native numeric text and source line.

pip install 'orfdata'
orfdata datasets download pfizer-atlas-dog-rna --version 2026-10-12.1
orfdata datasets query pfizer-atlas-dog-rna --sample 1 --unit counts

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()
dataset = registry.open("pfizer-atlas-dog-rna", "2026-10-12.1")
reference, = dataset.manifest.references
gene = ScopedTarget(reference, "gene", "ENSCAFG00845000002", "ensembl")
for observation in dataset.measurements(target=gene, unit="counts"):
    print(observation.sample_id, observation.value, observation.status)

All source gene IDs were checked against the checksum-pinned Ensembl 110 GTF. The import retains the source's coding and noncoding genes without a protein-coding filter. With that annotation already installed in PyEnsembl, construct the same target from a gene object:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

genome = EnsemblRelease(110, species="dog")
feature = genome.gene_by_id("ENSCAFG00845000002")
gene = ScopedTarget.from_pyensembl(feature, kind="gene", namespace="ensembl",
                                 context=reference)

An incompatible species, assembly or annotation release fails explicitly. There are 180 dog and 890 mouse annotation genes outside the measured count universe; querying one yields no observation, not a synthesized zero. Gene RNA abundance is context for a parent RNA and does not establish the abundance or translation of any particular uORF, ncORF or transcript isoform.

Samples retain original numeric SIDs, GEO/BioSample accessions, SRA runs, batches, native tissue labels and the public source metadata. Mouse libraries include 308 source-labelled c57 and 298 cd1 samples; these are biological strain labels, independent of the annotation reference. Donor IDs and sex are unknown at the deposited sample level. More specific GEO tissue labels remain alongside the count table's broader labels. There is no verified RNA-library-to-protein-pool crosswalk, so this release creates no assay pairs or protein-per-RNA ratios.

GSE325522, GSE325523 and GSE325525 each carry the same decompressed count matrix. ORFdata pins one input and records the equivalent mirrors instead of counting the data three times. The full matrix contains 2,183 nonhuman libraries. Although the metadata lists 44 human libraries, neither the native CSV nor the deposited human-ortholog RDS contains their counts. That source gap remains explicit. Rat, pig and macaque rows are present in the original matrix and remain candidates for separate releases through the same importer.

registry.build(name, source_paths=...) or orfdata datasets build NAME rebuilds from pinned counts, GEO metadata, factual Table S5 sample records and the historical GTF. Python returns a QuantitativeDataset ready to query. Reopen it offline with registry.open_build(name) or inspect it with registry.inspect_build(name). The CLI selects that source build explicitly with orfdata datasets query NAME --built; inspect --built checks its saved provenance and output receipt. Normal registry queries open the independently verified published artifact.

GEO data and Ensembl annotations retain their source reuse terms and attribution. The paper supplement has separate CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 terms; the original workbook is not bundled in the quantitative artifact. Source hashes, terms and processing details are in each manifest. All acquisition is explicit; installed queries and metadata discovery work offline.

docs.title: Build a reference proteome
docs.text:
A ReferenceTranscriptome names the transcript models in one installed PyEnsembl annotation. A Proteome selects protein products from those models: translations of the reference CDSs, catalogue ncORFs bound to the transcripts, and optionally viral proteins associated with the host. All three sources have annotations; reference_cds identifies the proteins induced by the reference annotation's CDS features. Each method returns a new proteome. proteome.layers records every addition with its role (host, viral, component, external, derived or filter), source, selection and counts, and each protein lists every transcript that encodes it.

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import Proteome, ReferenceTranscriptome

genome = EnsemblRelease(115, species="human")  # Installed with pyensembl install.
transcriptome = ReferenceTranscriptome.from_genome(genome)
reference_cds = transcriptome.proteome()                  # Default: all reference CDS isoforms.
one_per_gene = transcriptome.proteome(isoforms="longest")
proteome = transcriptome.proteome(nc_orf_sources="ms")            # Add MS-supported ncORFs.

The examples on this page continue that Python session. nc_orf_sources=() and viral=() are the defaults; a reference-only build does not load ncORF datasets. The ncORF argument accepts one string or a list:

Selection Included ncORFs [] or None None "all" Every compatible registered dataset, including optional ones "bundled" Every ORF in the bundled human dataset ["bundled", "ncorf-mammals-human"] The union of these datasets "ms" MS-supported ORFs across all compatible datasets ["proteomics", "ribosome"] ORFs with either kind of evidence across all compatible datasets ["bundled", "ms"] Every bundled ORF, plus MS-supported ORFs from the other datasets

Evidence rules and loaded ORFCatalog objects also work as sources. A list always takes the union; combine evidence rules with & when both are required. Species and assembly are taken from the transcriptome. Required datasets and liftover chains must already be installed. For all human datasets, run orfdata setup --species human --catalogs all once. Use "bundled" for the bundled data alone. The dataset loader/setup commands retain their own catalogue selectors; proteome() and Proteome.build() have only nc_orf_sources.

docs.title: Reference CDS proteins
docs.text:
transcriptome.proteome() and Proteome.from_genome(genome) take every transcript with a reference CDS protein sequence. For Ensembl this matches the annotation's protein FASTA: Ensembl 115 has 245,535 human proteins with 160,811 distinct sequences. They include nonsense-mediated-decay and immunoglobulin/T-cell receptor segment translations, and 11,540 proteins on patch, haplotype and unplaced contigs. Each protein records its accession, gene, transcript, contig and transcript biotype, so you can restrict them explicitly:

primary = {str(n) for n in range(1, 23)} | {"X", "Y", "MT"}
chromosomes = reference_cds.filter(lambda e: e.contig in primary, description="primary chromosomes")
print(len(chromosomes))

233995

filter records its description and the number of removed entries as a layer. Set isoforms="longest" on either constructor to choose one reference protein per gene. Selection uses amino-acid length without a terminal stop, then accession and transcript ID in lexical order to break ties. Every selected protein retains its original identifiers and occurrence. This is a length-based representative, not an Ensembl canonical or MANE designation. A missing gene ID raises an error. layers[0] records isoforms, the number available before selection and the number added.

Isoform selection applies only to reference CDS proteins. Added ncORFs retain all matching transcripts, and viral and derived proteins keep their own identities. Identical sequences from different genes remain separate entries.

Mouse, dog, yeast and other PyEnsembl species work the same way; mouse Ensembl 115 has 66,668 annotated proteins. orfdata does not download or index annotation data. An uninstalled genome raises an error naming the pyensembl install command.

docs.title: RefSeq proteins (experimental)
docs.text:
Build from NCBI's protein FASTA and genome-download feature table, with pinned byte checksums and an explicit ReferenceContext:

from orfdata import ReferenceContext

context = ReferenceContext(9615, "dog", "UU_Cfam_GSD_1.0", "NCBI RefSeq", "106",
                           assembly_accession="GCF_011100685.1")
reference = Proteome.from_refseq(
    "protein.faa.gz", "feature_table.txt.gz", reference=context,
    expected_sha256={"protein": protein_sha256, "feature_table": feature_table_sha256},
)
reference.save("dog.proteome.json.gz")

This preserves NCBI Gene IDs, versioned RNA/protein accessions, every mapped occurrence and all FASTA proteins. Wrong checksums, assemblies, missing proteins and conflicting assignments fail. CDS rows without protein products are counted in layers[0]["cds_without_protein"].

The annotated layer retains both asset hashes and identifier namespaces. Its genomic_spans maps each protein accession to spans in occurrence order. These are genomic envelopes, so occurrence CDS offsets/blocks and transcript biotypes remain unknown. No annotation indexing or downloads occur.

docs.title: Pinned Ensembl proteins
docs.text:
Proteome.from_ensembl() provides the same reference inventory and provenance contract for Ensembl's full GTF, peptide, cDNA and ncRNA files. It reads local plain or gzip files without building annotation indexes:

ReferenceContext.from_genome() from a matching PyEnsembl release is also accepted. Provider names Ensembl and ensembl are compared without case differences; the supplied context spelling is preserved in the snapshot.

context = ReferenceContext(9606, "human", "GRCh38", "Ensembl", "115",
                           assembly_accession="GCA_000001405.29")
reference = Proteome.from_ensembl(
    "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.pep.all.fa.gz",
    "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.115.chr_patch_hapl_scaff.gtf.gz",
    "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.cdna.all.fa.gz",
    "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.ncrna.fa.gz",
    reference=context,
    expected_sha256={"protein": protein_sha256, "gtf": gtf_sha256,
                     "rna": rna_sha256, "ncrna": ncrna_sha256},
)
reference.save("human.proteome.json.gz")

Obtain and pin the matching files from the same Ensembl release. The reader hashes the exact source bytes it parses. The GTF assembly accession, versioned transcript/protein accessions and versioned gene identities must agree with the supplied reference and sequence headers. Every peptide FASTA accession must have a GTF assignment and its exact RNA record; a missing coding sequence or conflicting duplicate fails the build. Identical protein sequences at different accessions and genes remain separate entries. Identical duplicate FASTA records are counted in the layer manifest. Protein residues, including Ensembl's internal stop symbols and ambiguous residues, are preserved exactly. Downstream prediction must assess whether it supports those sequences; the reference reader does not repair them.

The annotated layer carries all four source hashes, identifier namespaces and the complete protein inventory checksum. Its transcript_spans preserves each original genomic transcript envelope in occurrence order. These are not spliced CDS coordinates: occurrence start, end and coding_blocks remain unknown. Noncoding annotation transcripts without RNA bytes are listed explicitly in untranslated_transcripts_without_rna; they never become protein entries.

The same method accepts other species' matching Ensembl files and an explicit ReferenceContext. Reference membership does not establish RNA abundance, empirical translation, protein abundance or tissue restriction. The reader does not compare translations or transfer evidence between assemblies.

docs.title: Add ncORFs with selected evidence
docs.text:
Pass nc_orf_sources="ms", "ribosome", "all" or an evidence rule to proteome(), or add to an existing proteome with with_nc_orfs("ms"). Evidence presets query all compatible registered datasets, including optional ones. This selects catalogue ORFs by evidence and adds each one that a transcript of this genome encodes: the transcript contains the ORF's exact spliced coding path and translates to its protein. Counts below are for the bundled human catalogue (dataset 2026-10-11.1) and Ensembl 115. The table uses the lower-level load_catalog().query(evidence=...) notation; nc_orf_sources=None instead means no ncORFs:

Selection Human ORFs Encoded in Ensembl 115 evidence=None or "all": every catalogue ORF 7,264 7,239 evidence="ribosome" or "riboseq": translated in ribosome profiling 7,264 7,239 evidence="ms": any supporting MS peptide 2,186 2,181 evidence="immunopeptidomics": peptides eluted from MHC (in human, HLA) molecules 1,881 1,879 evidence="ms_unclassified": MS with an unreported assay type 537 535 evidence="proteomics": peptides from digested cellular proteins 73 72 "ms" with require_unique=True 1,623 1,621 "ms" with require_reviewed=True 44 44

All bundled ORFs come from ribosome-profiling catalogues, so "ribosome" selects all of them. An MS-supported ORF can have peptides from several assay types. require_unique keeps peptides that map to one protein within the MS source's search, which is not uniqueness across every possible protein; in this catalogue only the author HLA ligand mappings report it. require_reviewed keeps peptides with convincing community spectrum reviews. Because those two properties come from different sources, no bundled peptide has both. require_resolved excludes support that consists only of aggregate counts. See ORFs and evidence for the full definitions.

A list of evidence names selects ORFs with any of them: nc_orf_sources=["proteomics", "immunopeptidomics"] keeps ORFs with either kind of MS peptide, unlike "ms", which also counts unclassified MS. For ORFs that need two kinds of evidence at once, combine rules with &, below.

Length is a separate consumer policy, never an import rule. RibORF catalogues retain valid short source ORFs because they can matter for variant annotation even when they are unsuitable for a peptide search. Use catalog.query(min_protein_length=5), extra_orfs(..., min_protein_length=5), or:

search_reference = transcriptome.proteome(
    nc_orf_sources="ribosome", min_protein_length=5
)

The corresponding CLI option is --min-protein-length 5. A proteome snapshot's ncORF layer records both the threshold and length_filtered, so the omission is auditable and changes the cache identity. Reference CDS proteins are unaffected.

docs.title: Separate Ribo-seq and MS stringency
docs.text:
For more control, pass a rule. RiboSeq(min_studies=n) needs ribosome profiling in at least n independent studies the source names, and MS(min_peptides=n, unique=..., reviewed=..., mhc=...) needs at least n distinct supporting peptide sequences. MS(mhc=True) counts only peptides eluted from MHC molecules (the immunopeptidome) and MS(mhc=False) only peptides from digested cellular proteins (the whole proteome). MS() counts both, and the MS peptides whose source doesn't say which. methods= names the kinds directly, for combinations such as ("proteomics", "ms_unclassified"). & requires both rules and | accepts either:

from orfdata import MS, RiboSeq

reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(RiboSeq(min_studies=2))                        # replicated Ribo-seq
reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS())                 # Ribo-seq and MS
reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(RiboSeq(min_studies=2) | MS())                 # either
reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(RiboSeq() & MS(mhc=True))                     # Ribo-seq and an MHC ligand
reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(MS(methods=("proteomics", "ms_unclassified")))  # not immunopeptidomics-only
Rule Human ORFs Encoded in Ensembl 115 RiboSeq(min_studies=2) 3,085 3,072 RiboSeq(min_studies=3) 1,675 1,671 MS(min_peptides=2) 682 681 MS(methods=("proteomics", "ms_unclassified")) 610 607 RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS() 1,296 1,293 RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS(min_peptides=2) 457 456 RiboSeq(min_studies=2) \| MS() 3,975 3,960

GENCODE's c…riboseqorf… IDs are the 3,085 ORFs seen in two or more studies. Each method name above is the simplest rule: "ms" is MS(), "immunopeptidomics" is MS(mhc=True), "proteomics" is MS(mhc=False) and "ribosome" (or "riboseq") is RiboSeq(). The names before 0.28.0 ("shotgun", and "mhc" or "hla") still work, with a deprecation warning, and catalogues that use them still load. A peptide counts once however many assay types report it, and so do peptides that differ only by I and L (equal in mass). Nested peptides, such as MHC ligand length variants, count as one: the count is the largest set of supporting peptides none of which lies inside another, so a long peptide never hides two shorter, separate ones, and a stricter rule always selects a subset of a looser one. Of the 916 ORFs with two or more distinct peptide sequences, 234 have fewer than two that aren't nested. Each rule in & is checked on its own: MS(mhc=False) & MS(unique=True) needs a proteomics peptide and a unique peptide, not one unique proteomics peptide. A source's aggregate count stands for one observation: it satisfies RiboSeq() and MS() but never min_studies or min_peptides above 1, unique, reviewed or resolved=True. The layer stores the rule, so a snapshot records exactly how its ORFs were chosen; EvidenceRule.from_dict reads it back. Equal rules are stored the same way, whatever their order or repeats, so they give one proteome identity.

A translated ORF or a detected peptide does not by itself establish a stable, functional protein. Missing evidence does not establish that an ORF is never translated.

docs.title: Every transcript, and excluded ORFs
docs.text:
Each extra ORF produces one protein, whatever the number of transcripts encoding it. entry.occurrences lists them, the transcript the source names first. Each Occurrence has the transcript and gene, start and end slicing the transcript sequence, the genomic coding_blocks and on_source_transcript. Annotated entries have one occurrence, on their own transcript.

from collections import Counter

ms_orfs = [e for e in proteome if e.kind == "extra_orf"]
print(Counter(min(len(e.occurrences), 5) for e in ms_orfs))
print(Counter(e.reason for e in proteome.excluded))

Counter({5: 1253, 1: 345, 2: 254, 3: 184, 4: 145})
Counter({'ORF splice path mismatch': 5})

More than half of the MS-supported ORFs, 1,253 of 2,181, are encoded by five or more Ensembl 115 transcripts. The bundled models were validated against Ensembl 101, and later releases retire or change some of their transcripts. When an ORF's source transcript is gone or changed but another transcript still encodes it, the ORF is added and entry.source_binding gives the reason: 41 of the MS-supported ORFs, counted as not_on_source_transcript in the layer. The 5 in proteome.excluded are encoded by no Ensembl 115 transcript. identical_to_annotated in the layer counts added ORFs whose protein now matches an annotated protein; both entries are kept because they have different identities and evidence. proteome.by_sequence() groups entries with identical sequences, for example before an exact peptide search.

Source names resolve against the genome's species and assembly. "all" and evidence presets query every compatible registered dataset, using installed liftover chains where needed. "bundled" selects only the bundled human dataset. A missing dataset or chain raises with installation instructions; a species without a dataset cannot supply ncORFs. A loaded ORFCatalog, or a list of loaded catalogues, can also be passed directly as nc_orf_sources.

docs.title: Merging catalogues
docs.text:
Pass several catalogues for one species and assembly to use their ORFs together:

from orfdata import load_catalog, merge_catalogs

catalogs = [load_catalog(), load_catalog("study-orfs.json.gz")]  # The bundled one and a local file.
proteome = reference_cds.with_nc_orfs(catalogs)  # Or pass merge_catalogs(catalogs).

Records from different catalogues are one ORF when they have the same spliced coding path, protein, genetic code and start codon; declaring a start the code already uses, such as ATG, changes nothing. Records within one catalogue stay as it gave them. A record joins an ORF found on its own transcript before any other.

  • IDs. The merged ORF keeps the first catalogue's ID. Every source's record stays in record.members, and the others' IDs are in equivalent_ids as source:id. catalog.get and ExtraORFs.for_orf accept any of them.
  • ID collisions. When two sources use one ID for different ORFs, both become source:id, and the bare ID raises rather than picking one.
