Direct ORFCatalog(records, metadata) construction follows the same rule, retaining each native record in members without merging its evidence. IDs must still be unique within a source. If a source or native ID contains punctuation that would collide with a generated ID, generated components are percent-escaped; native IDs remain available through the source records. Use catalog.get("native-id", source="study") or orfs.for_orf("native-id", source="study") for explicit source selection. A combined string such as study:native-id raises if it also identifies another native record; explicit source selection resolves that ambiguity.
  • Evidence. Each source's evidence is kept, and evidence rules see the union: a peptide counts once per sequence. A Ribo-seq study two catalogues label differently counts once when their ribosome_study_pmids metadata give it the same PMID, as the bundled catalogue's does; without PMIDs it counts twice toward RiboSeq(min_studies=...).
  • Lookups. Queries by transcript, gene or biotype, for_transcript and ExtraORFs.for_gene(..., source=True) match every source's labels, and an ORF is on its source transcript when it is on any source's.
  • Annotation pins. Sources pinned to different annotation releases of the assembly leave the merged ORF unpinned; each member keeps its own pin.
  • Rejected merges. Catalogues must share a strain, where an unknown strain counts as its own value, and must not repeat a source, so two releases of one catalogue can't both be merged. A merged catalogue can be merged again.
  • Conflicts. catalog.metadata["conflicts"] lists ORFs that share a coding path but differ in protein, genetic code or declared start codon.

The layer's source joins the catalogues' releases, such as orfdata-catalog:2026-10-11.1+orfdata-catalog:study-v1. On the command line, repeat --nc-orf-sources FILE.

docs.title: Viral proteomes
docs.text:
Build one proteome with reference CDS proteins, every catalogue ORF that binds to the genome, and every distinct bundled viral protein set recorded for this host:

combined = transcriptome.proteome(nc_orf_sources="all", viral="all")
proteins_by_id = combined.by_accession()
combined.write_fasta("human-all-proteins.fasta")
combined.save("human-all-proteins.proteome.json.gz")

nc_orf_sources="all" includes every compatible registered dataset with no evidence filter. ORFs that do not bind to this genome are reported in combined.excluded. Reference CDS and viral proteins are unaffected.

proteins_by_id maps each unique protein accession to a ProteinSequence with its sequence, protein_source, taxon and source. by_sequence() groups entries with identical amino-acid sequences while retaining their separate identities. viral="all" chooses the native RefSeq placement when bundled references contain the same protein set at different DNA coordinate placements, as with HPV16. To request only one virus, use viral="HPV16" or an exact reference ID such as viral="NC_001526.4". with_viral("HPV16") accepts the same choices, as well as a ViralReference returned by viral_reference(...). Viral proteins are opt-in: a recorded host association does not mean every sample contains that virus. A virus without a recorded association to the host is rejected. Requesting viral="all" for a host with no bundled viral references raises instead of silently returning a host-only proteome.

ProteinSet represents named protein sequences supplied outside the bundled references. It has no virus or host behavior of its own. When the sequences are viral, pass the host association to with_viral so the same host check applies:

from orfdata import ProteinSet

# Template: substitute your FASTA, the virus taxon and your host-range source.
hpv16: ProteinSet = ProteinSet.from_fasta(
    "hpv16-proteins.fasta",
    name="HPV16",
    taxon_id=333760,
    source="Source database and release",
)
with_virus: Proteome = proteome.with_viral(
    hpv16,
    host_taxon_ids={9606},
    host_source="Host range source and date",
)

viral=[first, second] accepts several specific inputs. The tests exercise this with two synthetic viruses; HPV16 is the only released biological viral reference at present.

All protein kinds use the same ProteinSequence and appear in the same Proteome. ProteinSet is an input, not a second output collection. Viral proteins keep the virus's taxon and a source label such as viral:HPV16@NC_001526.4; their layer records the source accession, checksum and host-range source. proteome.host() returns the host's own proteins without viral entries, for example as a self reference.

The same input type handles a selected donor, transgene or custom component. That is a separate operation because a component's source reference and the proteome it is selected for are different facts:

from orfdata import ProteinSet, Proteome, ReferenceContext

human: ReferenceContext = ReferenceContext(
    9606, "human", "GRCh38", "Ensembl", "115"
)
mouse_reference: ReferenceContext = ReferenceContext(
    10090, "mouse", "GRCm39", "Ensembl", "115"
)
mouse: Proteome = Proteome(mouse_reference, ())
insert: ProteinSet = ProteinSet.from_fasta(
    "selected-human-insert.fasta",
    name="selected-human-insert",
    reference=human,
    source="Construct manifest 7",
)
chimera: Proteome = mouse.with_protein_set(
    insert,
    role="donor",
    target_taxon_ids={10090},
    target_source="Mouse line manifest 3",
)

This adds only the listed sequences, not the human proteome. The component layer retains the human source reference and the separate mouse-target assertion. No genomic placement, expression or sample membership is inferred. If the ProteinSet.reference exactly matches the proteome reference, the target assertion is unnecessary. Readding the same set is idempotent; changed content under the same name is rejected.

ProteinSet is deliberately sequence-only. It is suitable when the source has accessions, amino acids and provenance but no coordinate model. An ncORF source that has a transcript, coding path, initiation context or evidence belongs in an ORFCatalog/ORFRecord instead. Binding those ORF records to a reference produces the same ProteinSequence output in the same Proteome; the richer ORF facts are not flattened into a ProteinSet. Conversely, importing a bare ncORF protein FASTA as a ProteinSet does not invent a canonical ORF, alternative start, transcript placement or evidence.

docs.title: ncORFs with or without an installed transcriptome
docs.text:
If you have a PyEnsembl reference transcriptome, build a proteome containing only the ncORFs that bind to its transcripts:

nc_only = transcriptome.proteome(reference_cds=False, nc_orf_sources="all")
nc_only.write_fasta("reference-ncorfs.fasta")

orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --no-reference-cds --nc-orf-sources all --output reference-ncorfs.fasta

This uses the installed annotation and transcript sequences to check exact ORF paths. It does not read or include reference CDS proteins, and it does not need a whole-genome DNA FASTA. ORFs that do not bind are reported in nc_only.excluded.

If no transcriptome is installed, use the source ncORF catalogue directly; its source transcript and assembly identifiers remain attached, but no binding to a particular reference transcriptome is claimed:

from orfdata import load_catalog

catalog = load_catalog(species="human")
nc_orfs_by_id = {record.orf_id: record for record in catalog.query(evidence="all")}

orfdata --species human --evidence all --format fasta > nc-orfs.fasta

For viral source records alone, use viral_references(host="human") and each reference's .products and .orfs; this also needs no PyEnsembl genome:

from orfdata import viral_reference

ref = viral_reference("NC_001526.4")
viral_by_id = {orf.orf_id: orf for orf in ref.orfs}

The released collection currently has HPV16 in two DNA coordinate placements. Specifying viral= in Proteome.build only applies when building a host proteome. With an installed genome, filter entries by kind to obtain only extra_orf or only viral proteins; the result retains write_fasta, by_accession, and save.

nc_only = combined.filter(lambda entry: entry.kind == "extra_orf")
virus_only = combined.filter(lambda entry: entry.kind == "viral")

docs.title: Sample-derived proteins
docs.text:
Protein origin and sample-specific sequence changes are separate. A changed reference CDS protein or ncORF retains its parent protein source, while its derivation names the parent accession, sample and change IDs. Supply the amino acid sequence yourself; orfdata does not infer it from a VCF or claim that the sample expresses it:

from orfdata import DerivedProtein

altered = DerivedProtein(
    accession="sample-A:protein-1",
    sequence=altered_amino_acids,
    parent_accessions=("ENSP00000269305.4",),
    sample_id="sample-A",
    change_ids=("source-variant-id",),
    source="variant-caller-and-translation-release",
)
sample_proteome = combined.with_derived_proteins(altered)
sample_proteome.write_fasta("sample-A-proteins.fasta")

The parent must already be in the proteome. A derived protein has kind="derived" and protein_source inherited from its host parent (mixed for parents from different sources); entry.derivation stores the parent, its gene/transcript identifiers, sample, changes and optional source asset SHA-256. Its FASTA header includes sample, derived_from, parent_genes, parent_transcripts, changes and the supplied source. When a parent maps to several transcripts, pass parent_transcript_ids=(...,) to select the transcript for each parent; omitting an ambiguous choice raises. Reference transcript coordinates and reference protein measurements are not copied onto the altered sequence. Viral parents are not supported for derived proteins. The snapshot retains the complete derivation record.

docs.title: Proteins supplied by other tools
docs.text:
An adapter for an RNA assembly or DNA prediction can submit its amino-acid sequence without naming an included parent protein. It supplies source claims as ProducerInfo; these do not create genomic Occurrence mappings:

from orfdata import ProducerInfo, ProteinSequence

reference = transcriptome.proteome()
rna_product: ProteinSequence = ProteinSequence.from_producer(
    "MPEPTIDE",
    producer=ProducerInfo(
        origin="nc_orf", method="rna_assembly", tool="isovar",
        tool_version="2.0", native_id="ASM42", sample_id="sample-A",
        gene_names=("GENE1",), reference=reference.reference,
        start_complete=False, stop_complete=None,
    ),
)
joint = reference.with_proteins([rna_product])
joint.save("joint.proteome.json.gz")

origin describes the source protein or ORF category; method and tool describe how the supplied sequence was produced. The protein keeps provider, export paths, sample/run, native record, gene/transcript/ORF IDs, source hash and known reference when supplied. Its accession qualifies the native ID by producer and sample, so two samples can reuse the same native ID. Equal amino acid sequences stay distinct entries. Readding the same record is idempotent; changing content under the same identity raises.

The wrapper that serialized a producer record is provenance, not part of its source identity. Supply exporters=("isovar",) or exporters=("vaxrank",). Merging direct and wrapped copies produces one protein and one source record with exporters == ("isovar", "vaxrank"). The singular exporter= constructor argument remains readable for snapshots and callers from 0.35, but new code should use exporters.

Build a standalone producer collection with Proteome.from_proteins(proteins, reference=reference.reference), then use reference.merge(producer_collection). If a producer does not know its exact reference, the caller must explicitly choose compatibility="allow_unknown" when adding it to a known host reference. A standalone collection with mixed or unknown references uses Proteome.from_proteins(proteins, compatibility="mixed"); merging it into a host reference also requires an explicit compatibility choice. Known wrong species or reference declarations always fail. These collection operations preserve source entries through offline save/load.

An externally supplied fragment may use taxon_id=None when its source did not state a taxon. Its snapshot keeps None and its FASTA token says taxon=unknown. Adding it to a known host requires compatibility="allow_unknown"; that policy is stored separately and does not rewrite the source taxon. A known conflicting taxon still fails.

docs.title: Producer records and evidence
docs.text:
ProteinSequence carries amino acids. A producer can also attach versioned records for translations, evidence, events and outcomes that have no sequence. ORFdata stores these records in the snapshot without importing the producing package or interpreting its namespaced payload:

from orfdata import ProducerLink, ProducerRecord

translation = ProducerRecord(
    namespace="isovar", schema_version="export.v2", kind="translation",
    native_id="T1", sample_id="sample-A", payload={"cdna_id": "C1"},
)
evidence = ProducerRecord(
    namespace="isovar", schema_version="export.v2", kind="evidence",
    native_id="reads-1", sample_id="sample-A", support="rna_sequence",
    scope={"sample": "sample-A", "read_set": "R1"},
    payload={"read_count": 7},
)
unresolved = ProducerRecord(
    namespace="isovar", schema_version="export.v2", kind="event",
    native_id="E2", sample_id="sample-A", status="capped",
    complete=False, limits={"max_hypotheses": 4},
)
joint = joint.with_records(
    [translation, evidence, unresolved],
    links=[
        ProducerLink(translation.key, rna_product.accession, "protein", "translates_to"),
        ProducerLink(evidence.key, translation.key, "record", "supports_translation"),
    ],
)

The evidence record says it supports an RNA sequence. Its link to a translation does not claim that the protein was observed. A producer reporting a protein observation should use a separate evidence record with an explicit support type and observation scope. Two translations may link to one protein, and one evidence record may link to several translations; merging the same record again does not add its read count again.

An event may have status zero_product, unknown, filtered, incomplete or capped without a protein link. complete and limits retain the producer's search boundary. These status strings and the versioned payload belong to the producer; ORFdata retains unknown namespaces and versions exactly. Each record keeps its native ID separately from its qualified key. Links must resolve to records or proteins in the same proteome. Saving and loading preserve all records and links, and changing either changes the proteome identity.

docs.title: Save and reload
docs.text:
identity = proteome.save("human-e115.proteome.json.gz")
same = Proteome.load("human-e115.proteome.json.gz")  # Offline: no genome or catalogue needed.
assert same.identity == identity

A new save uses snapshot schema v5. load also reads existing v1–v4 snapshots. Loading v4 producer data normalizes exporter-specific protein and record keys to the shared source identity and retains the export path.

A snapshot holds every protein with its occurrences and evidence, the layers with their selections and catalogue identities, and the excluded ORFs. identity is the SHA-256 of that content, so it changes when any sequence, occurrence, selection, catalogue or exclusion changes, but not with file compression or formatting. Loading rejects a snapshot whose content does not match its identity, host proteins from another species, viral proteins without a matching host layer and layers declaring another reference. The human Ensembl 115 proteome with MS-supported ORFs is a 57 MB snapshot that saves in about 8 s and loads in about 11 s. Saving is deterministic: the same proteome gives the same bytes.

docs.title: Cache a built proteome
docs.text:
ReferenceTranscriptome.proteome delegates to Proteome.build. Both default to reference CDS proteins, then add only the requested ncORFs and viruses. The equivalent incremental methods are from_genome(isoforms=...), with_nc_orfs(nc_orf_sources) and with_viral(viral). viral= accepts "all"/True, a virus type, exact bundled reference ID, ViralReference, or a sequence of those specific inputs. with_viral also accepts an external ProteinSet when it is accompanied by host_taxon_ids= and host_source=; bundled references already carry those facts. With cache=True it keeps the result in the OpenVax DataCache root (ORFDATA_CACHE, OPENVAX_DATA_CACHE, or cache_root=). cache_root= is also where the species' registered catalogue is looked for, with or without cache=True:

proteome = transcriptome.proteome(nc_orf_sources=RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS(), cache=True)

The cache key includes the reference, isoform selection, evidence rule, catalogue and viral identities, snapshot schema and orfdata version. A later identical build, from any program, loads that verified snapshot, so tools share one identity. Earlier bundled-only measurements on Ensembl 115 took about 30 s for the first build, including saving, and about 7 s for later builds. Loading the optional datasets adds time and memory before the cache lookup. A cached snapshot is checked by its DataCache checksum, so it skips the re-serialization load does. Local annotation files of a custom genome are fingerprinted by size and SHA-256, so genomes that share names never share a protein. Proteins of a cached or loaded proteome don't carry orf; use extra_orfs(genome) for ORF objects. Each cached build sits next to a recipe.json recording its key and identity. Nothing is downloaded. reference_cds=False omits reference CDS proteins; nc_orf_sources=() is the reference-only default. Use proteome(reference_cds=False, nc_orf_sources="all") for only ncORFs bound to this transcriptome. viral="all" adds every distinct bundled viral proteome for this host. nc_orfs, catalog, catalogs, evidence, nc_orf_evidence, extra_orf_evidence, annotated, extra_orfs and host_sources are no longer constructor arguments. The lower-level with_extra_orfs(evidence, catalog=...) method remains available for existing callers that query a supplied catalogue with a separate evidence rule.

docs.title: Lower-level ORF lookup
docs.text: extra_orfs(genome, evidence=None) returns every catalogue ORF on every transcript carrying it, as TranscriptORF objects, with source_failures and excluded. Its default selects no evidence level: use it for annotation, such as variant effects on uORFs, where the proteome's MS default would be the wrong scope. Look ORFs up with for_transcript and for_gene; see identifiers for how versions and references are checked. for_transcript(transcript, include_annotated=True) adds the annotated CDSs on that transcript, and overlapping(...) finds ORFs at a genomic interval.

docs.title: An annotation for the ncORFs
docs.text:
write_annotation writes the proteome's ncORFs as a GTF with the matching transcript and protein FASTAs, so PyEnsembl-based tools can place a variant inside an ncORF and translate it:

written = combined.write_annotation("ncorfs")
print(written["annotation_gtf"], written["transcript_count"])

orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources ms \
  --output proteins.fasta --annotation ncorfs/

One coding transcript per ncORF is placed on its host gene, named by the catalogue's orf_id, with the ORF's spliced coding sequence and its translation. Reference CDS entries are left out, because the reference annotation already describes them, and viral entries are too, because they are not placed on this genome. Downstream tools shows how to read the result, alone or concatenated with the assembly's own annotation.

docs.title: FASTA headers
docs.text:
write_fasta writes 60-column sequences and, by default, one FASTA record per source protein. The first whitespace-delimited token has the same policy for reference CDS, ncORF, viral and supplied proteins:

>origin=nc_orf|orf=uORF|method=rna_assembly|tool=isovar|gene=GENE1|aa=8|taxon=9606|source=producer%3Aisovar|sample=T1|id=ASM42|key=... kind=external protein_source=nc_orf ...

The key suffix is a 16-character digest of the source-qualified accession; it disambiguates records without replacing the readable origin, ORF kind, method, tool, gene, amino-acid length, source, sample and native ID. Producer tokens also carry available tool version, provider, export paths and exact reference, plus start and stop as true, false or unknown. Optional run and gene_count fields appear when needed. gene=unknown means no gene was supplied. Multiple gene names appear as a comma-separated value with gene_count; punctuation and whitespace inside values are percent-escaped with UTF-8, including |, =, commas and spaces. orf=unknown means the producer did not state an ORF category. Supplied products may set ProducerInfo.orf_kind (for example uORF).

The complete source-qualified accession and original native ID stay in the snapshot. After Proteome.load, proteome.fasta_index() maps every FASTA first token to a tuple containing its source protein. A token collision raises before writing. write_fasta(..., deduplicate=True) groups exactly equal amino-acid sequences; its neutral token gives the record count, length and a group key without borrowing one producer's metadata, and fasta_index(deduplicate=True) maps it to every contributing protein. This option never groups a partial sequence with a longer sequence that contains it. Its description lists every source accession and the distinct protein sources and taxa. Keep the snapshot beside the FASTA to recover all producer records, evidence and no-sequence outcomes.

Additional key=value fields follow the first token in the description. All values are percent-escaped, so whitespace, |, = and newlines in source metadata cannot add fields or FASTA records. Producer descriptions include tool version, provider, export paths, native ID, exact reference, source checksum and explicit start/stop completeness. protein_source uses reference_cds, nc_orf, protein_set, viral or the producer's declared origin. The older kind field remains in FASTA and snapshots for compatibility; annotated there means a reference CDS protein and extra_orf means a catalogue ncORF. For extra ORFs, the native accession is the source ORF ID, transcript is its host transcript in this genome, and gene, gene_name and transcript_biotype describe that transcript in this genome. orf_type is the source's ORF category, kept verbatim; see ORF categories. evidence lists the supporting evidence types. transcripts counts the encoding transcripts when there are several, and source_transcript names the source's transcript when the header's transcript is a different one, as for ABLIM1 above, whose source transcript is gone. See also identifiers. The snapshot keeps every occurrence; the FASTA header shows the first. For bundled viral proteins, source names the exact viral reference; gene_name and product are the source's protein labels. A supplied protein FASTA may lack those annotations. For supplied derived proteins, derived_from links to their parent accessions, and parent_genes and parent_transcripts label those parents without asserting that their reference coordinates still describe the changed sequence. The FASTA header shows one host transcript and a count when several encode an entry; it does not list every occurrence, evidence record, source checksum or host-range attribution. Save a .proteome.json.gz snapshot alongside FASTA when those details must be recovered exactly.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --output human-e115.fasta
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --isoforms longest --output human-one-per-gene.fasta
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources all
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources all --viral all --output human-all-proteins.fasta --snapshot human-all-proteins.proteome.json.gz
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --viral HPV16 --output human-hpv16.fasta
orfdata proteome --species mouse --release 115
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --no-reference-cds --nc-orf-sources all
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --no-reference-cds --viral HPV16

The default is reference CDS proteins with all isoforms. --isoforms longest selects one per gene. --nc-orf-sources accepts the same string selections as Python, or a local JSON/JSON.gz dataset file. Repeat the option or use commas to combine sources:

orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources bundled,ncorf-mammals-human
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources ms --nc-orf-sources ribosome
orfdata proteome --species human --release 115 --nc-orf-sources my-orfs.json.gz

The separate --catalog, --catalogs and evidence-selection flags were removed from this command. For composed evidence rules use the Python argument, e.g. nc_orf_sources=RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS().

--viral all adds each distinct bundled viral protein set associated with the host, choosing its native placement when equivalent references exist. Use --viral with an exact reference ID to choose a placement; repeat the option for several specific viruses.

The FASTA goes to --output or standard output; --snapshot FILE also saves a snapshot, and --cache reuses or keeps the build in the cache; --cache-root DIR chooses the cache, for catalogues as well as builds. A JSON summary of the layers, identity and excluded ORFs goes to standard error.

docs.title: Not yet included
docs.text: Mouse noncanonical ORFs come from Chang et al.'s and Yang et al.'s Ribo-seq and OpenProt's MS catalogues once you install them; see Mouse. Dog noncanonical ORFs, and translated endogenous retrovirus (ERV) ORFs without annotated transcripts, need new source data; see the data roadmap. Products from circular RNAs, stop-codon readthrough or non-AUG starts can be described with TranscriptORF.at and SourceRNA (see the examples), but no bundled catalogue supplies them yet, so proteomes do not include them.

docs.title: ORFs and evidence
docs.text: The bundled human catalogue is the GENCODE Ribo-seq ORF Phase 1 set: 7,264 GRCh38 ORFs that ribosome-profiling studies found translated but that the reference annotation (GENCODE v35) did not annotate as proteins. 2,186 also have supporting MS peptides. "Noncanonical" is relative to an annotation and transcript: in Ensembl 115, 34 of the 7,108 ORFs that bind encode a protein identical to an annotated ENSP, and an ORF can be annotated in one transcript model but not another. The catalogue is source-backed; it does not discover every possible ORF. The larger Phase 2 set is planned (#16). Most users start with a reference proteome or extra_orfs(genome); this page describes the objects and evidence underneath.

docs.title: ORF categories
docs.text:
Each ORF keeps its source category verbatim as orf_type. The terms follow Mudge et al. 2022, Table 2:

orf_type Position uORF Within the 5′ UTR of a protein-coding gene's transcript uoORF Begins in the 5′ UTR and overlaps the annotated coding sequence in a different frame intORF Entirely within the annotated coding sequence, in a different frame dORF Within the 3′ UTR doORF Begins within the annotated coding sequence and ends in the 3′ UTR, in a different frame lncRNA On a transcript annotated as a long noncoding RNA processed_transcript On a transcript annotated as processed_transcript, with no annotated protein

The category, the host transcript's biotype and the evidence are separate properties. The category describes the source's annotation; a bound ORF's transcript.biotype describes the annotation you loaded. In Ensembl 115, for example, most processed_transcript ORFs are on protein_coding_CDS_not_defined or retained_intron transcripts, and 48 uORFs are on nonsense-mediated-decay transcripts. One RNA can carry several ORFs.

docs.title: Objects and queries
docs.text:
A TranscriptORF is one ORF placed on one RNA, including its ordinary annotated CDS, catalogue ORFs, and source-defined ORFs. It connects the coding sequence and protein to that RNA's coordinates for variant interpretation, RNA evidence and proteome export. The RNA may be a PyEnsembl transcript or a SourceRNA, and one RNA may carry several ORFs. Canonical transcript selection is independent of the ORF placement. ReferenceORF is the same class under its original name. Each has:

  • kind: "annotated" for an annotated CDS, "extra_orf" for a catalogue or source-defined ORF.
  • record: optional catalogue provenance. An annotated CDS or an ORF constructed with TranscriptORF.at has record=None and is still a valid TranscriptORF.
  • orf_id: the source ORF ID, or the versioned protein ID of an annotated CDS.
  • start and end: Python slice coordinates into the transcript's spliced sequence, so transcript.sequence[orf.start:orf.end] == orf.coding_sequence. The coding sequence includes the stop codon when there is one. The genomic path is in coding_blocks, 1-based and inclusive.
  • transcript, transcript_id, gene, gene_id and gene_name: the transcript carrying the ORF and its gene in the annotation you loaded.
  • source_transcript_id, source_gene_id and source_gene_name: what the ORF's source says, and on_source_transcript: whether this is that transcript.
  • protein_sequence, orf_type, model and evidence. An annotated CDS has no orf_type, model or evidence of its own.
  • start_complete and stop_complete: independent True, False or None (unknown) boundary states. coding_phase is the number of leading bases before the first complete codon, or None if the frame is unknown. For an annotated CDS, equivalent_ids: other annotated proteins with the identical placement.

A catalogue ORF is checked strictly: the assembly, available species information, the full spliced coding path, the protein sequence and the terminal stop must all match. An annotated CDS is taken as the annotation defines it, with the annotation's protein. Annotations include selenoproteins and CDSs without marked start or stop codons, so translation is not re-checked; start_complete and stop_complete report what the annotation marks.

For a source-defined fragment, TranscriptORF.at(rna, start, end=end, phase=phase, start_complete=False, ...) retains its exact interval on the parent RNA. Phase is 0, 1 or 2 leading bases (INSDC codon_start - 1). Leading and trailing partial codons remain in coding_sequence and coding_positions; the protein contains only translated complete codons. A known local frame does not imply a known initiation site. Pass None for an unknown start or stop boundary. Supplied protein sequences and known stop declarations are checked against the interval.

TranscriptORF.from_dict(orf.to_dict(), rna) restores the placement against an explicitly supplied RNA, checking its identity, reference, coding path and sequence fingerprints. It preserves source evidence and optional catalogue provenance.

Every to_dict() export includes resolved_transcript.contig and resolved_transcript.strand, including annotated CDSs and TranscriptORF.at placements whose model and record are null. These fields describe the RNA actually carrying the ORF, preserving its contig spelling and +/- strand; they do not substitute the original source model's locus. Unknown SourceRNA locus values remain null, so unknown orientation is explicit. Saved results can be interpreted without reloading a reference sequence.

These are additive fields in orfdata.transcript_orf.v1 as of 0.42.1. The reader accepts older v1 exports where they are absent. If a field is present, including an explicit null, it must match the supplied carrier RNA during replay.

from orfdata import extra_orfs

orfs = extra_orfs(genome)  # Every catalogue ORF, on every transcript carrying it.
tpst1 = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000304842")
for orf in orfs.for_transcript(tpst1, include_annotated=True):
    print(orf.kind, orf.orf_id, orf.orf_type, orf.start, orf.end, len(orf.equivalent_ids))

extra_orf c7riboseqorf56 uORF 149 269 0
annotated ENSP00000302413.5 None 290 1403 21

Results come in RNA order: the uORF ends 21 bases before the annotated CDS starts, and 21 other proteins share TPST1's annotated placement exactly. Another transcript's CDS is listed only when this RNA encodes the same ORF. A CDS without a marked start or stop codon, such as a fragment on a truncated transcript, is listed only when this RNA continues identically beyond that end; otherwise translation would read on. Two such TPST1 fragments are not listed here. annotated_orfs(transcript) gives just the annotated ones; TranscriptORF.from_annotation(transcript) gives one transcript's own CDS.

orfs.overlapping(contig, start, end, genome_build=...) finds ORFs whose coding path overlaps a 1-based inclusive genomic interval; introns between coding blocks don't count. Add include_initiation_context=True to include an ORF's spliced start flanks, for example for a Kozak-position variant. Flanks come from the transcript each placement is on (orf.initiation_context), since transcripts sharing a coding path can differ upstream of the start codon.

docs.title: Transcripts carrying an ORF
docs.text:
An ORF is placed on every transcript that contains its exact spliced coding path and translates to its protein, not only on the transcript its source names. In Ensembl 115 the bundled ORFs have 67,529 such placements; only 1,314 ORFs are carried by a single transcript. on_source_transcript marks the one the source names. Another carrying transcript is not evidence that the ORF is translated from it, and the ORF's evidence is the same on every placement.

orfs.source_failures lists ORFs whose source transcript is absent from this annotation or no longer carries them, with the reason. Most are still placed elsewhere: of 156 such ORFs in Ensembl 115, only the 25 in orfs.excluded are carried by no transcript. record.bind(transcript) still binds strictly to the source's transcript.

Annotated CDSs can also lie in other transcripts. MIURF's CDS sits in the "5′ UTR" of MIEF1's mRNA, for example, and SNURF's in SNRPN's:

mief1 = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000325301")
for orf in orfs.for_transcript(mief1, include_annotated=True):
    print(orf.kind, orf.orf_id, orf.source_gene_name, orf.start, orf.end, orf.on_source_transcript)

extra_orf c22riboseqorf42 MIEF1 72 132 True
annotated ENSP00000490747.1 MIURF 176 389 False
annotated ENSP00000327124.2 MIEF1 487 1879 True
extra_orf c22norep69 MIEF1 527 677 True

MIURF's protein keeps its own ID and gene while sitting on MIEF1's RNA, so it is not mistaken for a new protein. The examples cover non-AUG starts, recoded stop codons, frameshifts, circular RNAs, precursor products and IRES elements.

docs.title: Catalogue records
docs.text:
load_catalog() loads the bundled human records offline using only the Python standard library; like PyEnsembl, it defaults to species="human". catalog.for_transcript(transcript) binds the catalogue ORFs on one transcript. To inspect source records without a genome:

from orfdata import load_catalog

catalog = load_catalog()
records = catalog.query(gene="TPST1", evidence="ms")

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
Bundled ORF IDs are the source's GENCODE Phase I IDs. They start with the chromosome: c7riboseqorf56 is on chromosome 7. The 3,085 c…riboseqorf… ORFs were detected in two or more ribosome-profiling studies, and the 4,179 c…norep… ORFs in one. They are not Ensembl stable IDs.

Each record names one host transcript (transcript_id, an unversioned ENST) and that transcript's gene (gene_id, an ENSG), as validated against Ensembl 101. For an ORF on an mRNA, this is the gene of the transcript's annotated protein. Later releases can change both: of the 7,108 ORFs that bind to Ensembl 115, 87 host transcripts now belong to a different ENSG and 796 gene symbols changed. A bound ORF's gene_id, gene_name and transcript describe the genome you loaded; orf.model keeps the source's labels. In extra_orfs(genome), for_gene matches genes in the loaded annotation, or the source's labels with source=True. for_transcript and for_gene reject a transcript or gene from another reference, and a versioned Ensembl ID must match the loaded version.

The host is one of possibly several transcripts that carry the same ORF; see transcripts carrying an ORF.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Use orf.evidence.has_evidence("ribosome") (or "riboseq"), "proteomics" (peptides from digested cellular proteins), "immunopeptidomics" (peptides eluted from MHC molecules; HLA in human), or "ms" (any supporting MS observation). Source observations whose MS assay type is unspecified remain labelled "ms_unclassified". Catalogues from before 0.28.0 say "shotgun", "mhc" and "hla"; they load with the current names.

orf.evidence.has_evidence("ms", require_unique=True, require_reviewed=True)

This requires a supporting spectrum review and a single protein mapping within that source's search scope. It does not imply uniqueness across every possible protein. Inspect orf.evidence.peptides for peptide sequences, source accessions, matching intervals, mapping counts and review quality. Missing counts remain unknown; low or mixed spectrum reviews do not count as supporting MS.

has_evidence and catalog.query(evidence=...) also take rules that set Ribo-seq and MS stringency separately, such as RiboSeq(min_studies=2) & MS(min_peptides=2); see Build a reference proteome.

Some sources provide only aggregate support counts. EvidenceSummary keeps the native metric, definition, value, source/release, source checksum and explicitly scoped entity. For example, OpenProt's native metrics include an MS score that sums study-specific unique-peptide counts; it is neither global peptide uniqueness nor protein abundance. Its translation score counts studies with significant translation detection. None means unknown and remains distinct from a reported zero.

Positive summaries in orf.evidence.summaries can satisfy general evidence queries. To require actual peptide records or named ribosome studies, use:

orf.evidence.has_evidence("ms", require_resolved=True)
catalog.query(evidence="ribosome", require_resolved=True)

The CLI uses --evidence ms --require-resolved. The orfdata query command also takes the Ribo-seq and MS requirements of orfdata proteome:

orfdata --min-ribo-seq-studies 2 --min-ms-peptides 2 --format tsv
orfdata --gene TPST1 --min-ribo-seq-studies 2 --min-ms-peptides 1 --either

Uniqueness and review filters always require resolved peptide observations. Summaries never create peptide sequences, residue coverage, retained variant peptides or mutant-translation evidence. Their protein checksum and species/reference checks prevent attaching them to a different protein or incompatible source context.

A sequence-level summary may have several transcript assignments. Those records share the summary's key; catalog.evidence_summaries returns each native metric once and rejects conflicting facts for the same identity. Native accession aliases must be resolved explicitly by the source adapter. Counts from different metrics and sources are not summed, and a later peptide-resolved snapshot is not an additional independent experiment merely because it has more detail.

The OpenProt mouse catalogue uses these summaries. OpenProt's human and yeast files are not imported yet; see #18.

The distinction between translation, peptide detection and functional protein evidence follows the TransCODE study. Source evidence stays at its declared ORF or protein-sequence scope. It is not automatically evidence for another isoform, a mutant protein, a fusion or another species.

docs.title: Variants and RNA products
docs.text:
Varcode keeps the reference object alongside its modification:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease
from orfdata import load_catalog
from varcode import Variant, annotate_orf_variants

genome = EnsemblRelease(95, species="human")  # already downloaded and indexed
transcript = genome.transcript_by_id("ENST00000304842")
orf, = load_catalog().for_transcript(transcript)
variant = Variant("7", 66205486, "C", "G", genome=genome)
annotation = annotate_orf_variants([variant], orf)
assert annotation.reference is orf
print(annotation.effect)  # P2A in the TPST1 upstream ORF
result = annotation.to_dict()  # reference, evidence and altered products

Isovar's annotate_sv_orf_evidence attaches the same reference annotations to reconstructed RNA products and preserves each candidate's RNA support. For example, the native TPST1 peptide KIILSKISV is absent from the Sid TPST1–CRCP alternatives, so its MS evidence does not support those altered products.

The reference integration, including strict reference-context validation, is available in Varcode 10.13.0 and Isovar 1.51.0.

docs.title: Data and limits
docs.text:
The bundled human GRCh38 catalogue, dataset 2026-10-11.1, draws on the GENCODE Phase I reference, TransCODE author exports, and the community microprotein spectrum benchmark. All 7,264 ORF paths and proteins were checked against Ensembl 101 GTF, coding RNA and noncoding RNA FASTAs. The 2,186 models with supporting MS observations use the packaged source-specific filters; this is not a count of proven functional proteins. Packaged manifests retain source accessions, checksums, licenses, processing rules and dataset version.

Catalogue models bind as complete ORFs with a terminal stop under NCBI tables 1, 2 or 3 and their initiation codons, or a start codon the model declares with start_codon; see genetic codes. All bundled models use table 1 and start at ATG. Transcript-boundary contexts can be partial; initiation efficiency and effects on the main coding region are not established by these data.

ORFs that a source defines on an RNA rather than in genomic coordinates use TranscriptORF.at: non-AUG starts, fragments without a known start, stop codons read through, and ORFs on circular or other source RNAs (SourceRNA). See the examples. The bundled catalogue contains none of these. Fusions, edited RNAs and programmed frameshifts in catalogue models need further model support, and ORF discovery is outside the current API.

load_uorf_catalog() preserves Isovar's upstream-only snapshot: 3,771 models, dataset 2026-10-08.2. New code should use the broader load_catalog() API.

docs.title: Other species
docs.text:
ReferenceContext and ScopedTarget keep taxa, strains, assemblies and annotation versions separate. Custom genomes without species/taxonomy need an explicit context when binding; source-pinned contexts require an exact match for record.bind(transcript). With any_transcript=True, as extra_orfs uses to place ORFs by their exact coding path and protein, a record pinned to another annotation release of the same species, strain and assembly is also accepted. ORFs on another assembly can be lifted over.

load_catalog(species="mouse") returns a species' ORFs: the bundled catalogue, or those downloaded or built through CatalogRegistry, merged when there are several, as mouse's three are. genome_build= chooses the assembly. It never downloads, and for a species without a catalogue the error lists the catalogues that exist.

load_catalog(path) reads a custom versioned JSON catalogue. Each catalogue is scoped to one species and assembly; each model records its NCBI taxon, scientific name, assembly, translation table and source. Human evidence is never transferred to a mouse ortholog. Mouse ORFs come from OpenProt, Chang et al. and Yang et al., and each importer is tested with real source rows on real Ensembl transcripts.

To build a catalogue, create ORFModel objects from source coordinates and sequences, attach source observations with ORFRecord.from_model(model, evidence), and construct ORFCatalog(records, metadata). Its to_dict() produces the orfdata.catalog.v1 JSON representation. Genomic coding blocks are 1-based, inclusive, sorted by genomic position, and include the terminal stop codon.

The mouse catalogues come from pinned importers that check every row's coordinates and protein; see Mouse. OpenProt's human and yeast files are not imported yet.

docs.title: Rebuild and verify
docs.text:
From a development checkout with the PyEnsembl dependency installed:

python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m orfdata.build --source-dir /path/to/sources --prepare-sources \
    --all-orfs --output orfdata/data/orf-evidence
./lint.sh
./test.sh

Source preparation downloads pinned public inputs and needs Rscript to extract the author export. Ordinary queries need neither R nor spreadsheet libraries.

docs.title: Native protein search references
docs.text:
A search reference lists the sequences available to a particular MS search. It is independent of reported abundance or experimental evidence that a protein exists. ORFdata exposes the exact deposited FASTA, including unreported entries.

Dataset Search entries FASTA bytes, downloaded and installed pfizer-atlas-human-protein 20,600 13,831,073 pfizer-atlas-mouse-protein 21,989 14,325,720 pfizer-atlas-dog-protein 20,649 14,659,832

These are uncompressed, no-isoform UniProt search sets from data release 2026-10-12.1. The historical UniProt release and genomic assembly remain unknown. ORFdata does not replace them with a current proteome.

from orfdata import DatasetRegistry, ScopedTarget

registry = DatasetRegistry()
name, version = "pfizer-atlas-dog-protein", "2026-10-12.1"
spec, = registry.search_references(name, version)  # Metadata only; no I/O.
registry.download_reference(name, version)        # Explicit verified download.
search = registry.open_reference(name, version)   # Offline; raises if missing.

entry = search.get("A0A068LEV2")
print(entry.header, entry.sequence, entry.sequence_sha256)
assert search.membership(entry.target).status == "present"
for entry in search.entries():
    assert entry.target.reference == search.reference

absent = ScopedTarget(search.reference, "protein", "not-in-this-search", "uniprot")
assert search.membership(absent).status == "not_in_search"

Dog has 9,929 reported group representatives and 10,720 other search entries, including A0A068LEV2. Those other entries have no reported representative; that does not prove that their peptides were undetected. The summary table does not resolve all protein-group members. Query group abundance separately through dataset.measurements().

Membership accepts an explicitly scoped native protein target. A different reference raises an error. Other namespaces, ORFs, genes and protein groups return unknown: first supply an explicit, validated reference mapping. Search membership never creates a zero, allocates a group's abundance, establishes protein detectability, or supplies MHC presentation evidence. Exact accession lookup does not perform sequence matching or infer coverage of a new ORF.

Each entry retains its full header, FASTA ID, residues, sequence hash, source taxon, optional gene label and source line. search.spec.to_dict() records the dataset version, reference identity, sequence-set SHA-256, source URL, size, licence and attribution. The deposited records do not specify decoy/control roles; those fields stay None. UniProt records retain CC-BY-4.0 attribution.

orfdata datasets references pfizer-atlas-dog-protein --version 2026-10-12.1
orfdata datasets download-reference pfizer-atlas-dog-protein --version 2026-10-12.1
orfdata datasets inspect-reference pfizer-atlas-dog-protein --version 2026-10-12.1
orfdata datasets query-reference pfizer-atlas-dog-protein --version 2026-10-12.1 --target A0A068LEV2

Pin the quantitative dataset version and retain the matching search spec when exporting an analysis. Both use the same native ReferenceContext; select reference=spec.reference and asset_id=spec.source.asset_id if a dataset has multiple declared search sets (--reference KEY --asset ID in the CLI). Reference downloads use a separate DataCache store and never rebuild or download abundance. Local source overrides are checksum-verified; force=True creates a new immutable bundle and preserves already-open readers. Ordinary discovery, inspection and opening stay offline. Published quantitative hashes are unchanged.

The same reference model accepts any taxon, with no inferred cross-species joins. Adapters must explicitly declare their native search sets and formats. The initial parser supports deposited UniProt FASTAs. CoPY yeast's QconCAT FASTA is synthetic calibration material, so it is not exposed as a native yeast proteome; that historical search reference remains an explicit source gap.

docs.title: Historical Ensembl searches
docs.text: Declared Ensembl peptide FASTAs retain exact versioned identifiers and native headers, including alternate-reference entries and stop characters. Gzip source hashes identify the original compressed bytes. An Ensembl header does not encode taxonomy: source_taxon_id is None, while the explicit pinned reference retains the source species. Gene labels use the native gene symbol when present, otherwise the native versioned gene ID. No ID-version stripping or protein-detection claim is implicit in a search lookup. See the human tissue dataset.

docs.title: Source references and PyEnsembl mappings
docs.text:
A proteomics experiment may search a known protein FASTA without naming a genomic assembly. An older RNA study may report its annotation provider but omit the release. ORFdata keeps these source identities and their unknown fields.

from orfdata import ReferenceContext

source = ReferenceContext(
    taxon_id=9615, species="dog", genome_build=None,
    annotation_name="uniprot", annotation_version=None,
    sequence_sha256=searched_fasta_sha256,
)

Unknown assembly/provider fields require a pinned sequence_sha256 or source_sha256. The former identifies a sequence set; the latter can pin an input table when its reference release is unreported. These source contexts cannot bind a genomic transcript. A ReferenceORF still requires a complete genomic model validated against its actual PyEnsembl transcript. Existing complete-reference keys are unchanged.

docs.title: Query through an explicit mapping
docs.text:
ReferenceMapping connects a native ScopedTarget to all candidate targets in one destination reference. It records the dataset/version, mapping method, validation, source provenance, status and unresolved/unmapped reason. Importers must perform the stated checks against the pinned inputs. Unique identifier resolution is separate from sequence validation.

from orfdata import ScopedTarget

target = ScopedTarget.from_pyensembl(gene, kind="gene", namespace="ensembl:110")
for view in dataset.mapped_measurements(target):
    print(view.measurement.value, view.measurement.unit)
    print(view.measurement.target, view.requested_target)
    print(view.mapping.method, view.mapping.validation)

The view contains the original observation, including its source reference, target, sample, assay, unit and provenance. Nothing is relabeled or copied onto the requested target. Direct dataset.measurements(target=...) still returns only observations native to that exact target/reference.

By default, mapped queries return uniquely resolved assignments. Use mapping_statuses=["ambiguous", "unresolved"] to inspect other candidates, and require_sequence=True to require recorded exact sequence validation. A group value returned for a candidate member has attribution="group_membership_context"; it does not independently quantify that protein. Parent gene/transcript RNA cannot map directly onto an ORF. Use a separate parent-context relationship.

The CLI exposes the same query:

orfdata datasets query DATASET --mapped --reference ref:SHA256 \
    --kind protein --namespace ensembl:110 --target PROTEIN_ID --require-sequence

docs.title: Importer contract
docs.text:
Pass reference_mappings= to QuantitativeDataset.create. Declare source and destination contexts in the manifest. Each source/destination-reference pair has one mapping containing all candidates, preventing competing unique claims. Unmapped records remain visible through dataset.reference_mappings().

The status is unique, ambiguous, unmapped or unresolved. A single reported protein representative with incomplete group membership is unresolved; its measurement cannot become a uniquely measured member. Identifier-based mappings must say what was checked and leave sequence validation absent when unavailable. For an exact sequence search, record:

validation = {"sequence": {
    "source_sha256": source_protein_sequence_sha256,
    "target_sha256": matching_protein_sequence_sha256,
    "all_candidates_checked": True,
}}

These are hashes of the compared sequences, distinct from the whole searched FASTA's hash in the reference context. Both hashes must agree to count as an exact match. ORF assignments additionally require their own frame and position evidence. Known reference-strain differences need explicit strain_relationship evidence. Cross-species mappings use the separate orthology API.

Storage version 3 preserves these mappings. Earlier versions remain readable and report no declared reference mappings; no mapping is inferred on load.

docs.title: Species and references
docs.text:
Resolve names and IDs offline with orfdata.reference.species_taxon(name) and species_name_for_taxon(taxon_id). The latter returns a canonical species name, or None for an unknown positive ID, without requiring an Ensembl annotation.

ORFdata uses the same objects for human, mouse, dog, zebrafish, C. elegans, yeast and custom species. Every ORF states its NCBI species taxon, assembly and genetic code. A ReferenceContext also pins the annotation provider/version and can retain a versioned assembly accession, strain taxon/label and sequence-set SHA-256.

from orfdata import ReferenceContext, ScopedTarget

yeast = ReferenceContext(
    taxon_id=4932, species="saccharomyces_cerevisiae",
    genome_build="R64-1-1", assembly_accession="GCA_000146045.2",
    annotation_name="ensembl", annotation_version="115",
    strain="S288C", strain_taxon_id=559292,
)
target = ScopedTarget(yeast, "protein", "YFL039C", "ensembl:115")
print(target.key)

Target keys include the reference, source namespace, kind and source identifier. Identical local IDs in different species, reference versions or datasets remain separate. Known aliases such as canis_familiaris and canis_lupus_familiaris resolve to dog taxon 9615 through a versioned mapping; the original name stays in exports. Assembly names are never automatically equated, and strain identity is never discarded. Unknown species require their own explicit taxonomy context; they do not require a schema change.

ReferenceContext.from_genome(genome) resolves available PyEnsembl metadata offline. A custom Genome without species/taxonomy needs an explicit context:

bound = record.bind(transcript, context=yeast)
# Or: catalog.for_transcript(transcript, context=yeast)

The caller declares metadata absent from a custom genome; any metadata already present must agree. The binder still checks transcript version, strand, complete spliced path, coding sequence and protein. An ORF model with a reference_context requires that exact context. Older catalogues without a pinned annotation context can bind an identical transcript in another release; the actual resolved context and transcript/coding/protein hashes are exported. No binding downloads a reference or performs liftover.

context.validate_genome(genome) checks available metadata against an explicit context. Genomic alleles can use include_annotation=False: their coordinates are independent of a gene annotation release, while taxonomy, strain and assembly checks still apply. This does not relax ORF or RNA-product binding.

ScopedTarget supports genes, transcripts, ORFs, proteins, ambiguous protein groups and peptides. A parent's gene or RNA measurement remains at its original resolution; this identity layer does not copy it onto every ORF. Orthology and equal peptide sequences do not transfer observations between species.

docs.title: Genetic codes
docs.text:
Each ORF declares its NCBI translation_table. The binder supports complete stopped ORFs under table 1 (standard), table 2 (vertebrate mitochondrial) and table 3 (yeast mitochondrial), each with that table's NCBI initiation codons. An initiation codon reads as methionine only at the start. Other codes and initiation codons fail explicitly; there is no fallback to the standard code. A contig named MT never selects a code implicitly: a human mitochondrial ORF must declare table 2, and a yeast one table 3. See NCBI's code definitions.

bound.genetic_code returns the declared code. Tools that build modified products, such as Varcode and Isovar, must translate them with that code. For example, OpenProt's IP_306399 on human MT-ND4 begins ATA and ends AGG. It binds under table 2; table 1 would read those codons as isoleucine and arginine.

OpenProt import manifests can declare processing.translation_tables by exact native transcript ID, for example {"ENST00000361381.2": 2} for the qualified human IP_306399 row. The declaration belongs to the pinned source/reference manifest and is retained in catalogue provenance. Mitochondrial rows require such a declaration; unsupported codes and IDs absent from the input fail. The importer retains the native coordinate conversion and aggregate MS/TE counts. Binding still checks the exact transcript sequence and protein. This does not publish a complete human or yeast OpenProt catalogue (#18).

docs.title: Quantitative storage
docs.text:
ORFdata 0.8 writes compact SQLite storage version 4. Measurement, QuantitativeDataset, the registry and CLI keep the same public records and query semantics. Human, mouse, dog, yeast and arbitrary taxa retain separate reference-scoped identities.

References, targets and assays are stored once and addressed by internal integer keys. Measurements retain their values and metadata; repeated required fields are reconstructed from indexed columns and the dataset manifest. Fields equal to the fixed version-4 defaults are omitted from stored JSON and restored on read. Zeros, nulls, censoring, uncertainty, nested provenance and derived inputs retain their meaning. Foreign keys prevent cross-reference target/assay assignments. Internal integer keys never appear as public biological identifiers.

ORFdata 0.32 writes storage version 5, which also stores each target mapping's candidates as kind, identifier and namespace: they always share the mapping's reference, which its row already names. The dog DLA ligand dataset, with 62,492 mappings, is 255 MB, against 389 MB in the version 4 layout. Version 4 files remain readable, and a version 4 fixture written by the released ORFdata 0.30.0 tests that.

Published storage versions 1, 2, 3 and 4 remain readable. There is no automatic migration or replacement of downloaded artifacts. A new source rebuild can use a different storage layout and therefore a different file checksum while returning the same records. Registry downloads always verify the exact published artifact's hash; source builds retain their own DataCache receipts.

Large releases can distribute a tar.gz archive in ordered, checksummed parts. DatasetRegistry.download() installs these through DataCache's transactional archive support and still returns one dataset.sqlite. The registry pins every part, the assembled compressed archive, and the extracted SQLite bytes separately. Only that one regular file is permitted; extraction has an explicit size limit. The extracted hash and embedded dataset manifest are checked before publication and when an existing installation is reused. A failed refresh preserves readers of the previous installation. This requires DataCache 1.29.3 or later.

download_metadata() includes an archive definition for these releases. Local overrides use source_paths={"dataset.sqlite": [part0, part1, ...]} in the declared order. After installation, open() and inspect() remain offline and need neither the parts nor original build inputs. Checks use the registry's independent SQLite hash, so changing both cached bytes and a cache receipt cannot repin a release. verify_files=False skips content hashing but checks file type and size, and never reports cryptographic verification. Historical single-file releases retain their existing download paths.

A source asset may likewise declare metadata.archive, with its own hash and size describing the extracted file. Explicit source builds can acquire that component, or accept an ordered list of local part paths for its source override. A local extracted-file override still works. Opening a built dataset never acquires a component, and an already verified source build can be reused after the separate component cache has been removed.

The implementation streams observations and bounds its target cache to 131,072 entries. SQLite index statistics are populated during creation so a narrow target query can use the target index instead of scanning an entire reference. Raw SQL table layouts are internal; use the Python/CLI query and export APIs.

docs.title: Native peptide vectors
docs.text:
Canine native-evidence builds use storage version 6 for the common measurement API. Numeric vectors preserve their declared type, exact numeric bytes, independent presence bits and null-vector state. Sample/assay axes and native source records are stored once. Queries expand the requested cells into ordinary Measurement objects, retaining missing values, source record IDs, native units and provenance. Target and assay indexes select vectors before expansion. Counts report logical observations rather than stored vectors. Mapped/paired queries and Parquet export use the same projection. Opening and querying a release never accesses the remote vendor file or requires the extraction dependencies.

The native evidence component declares its own encoding version. Version 2 stores scalar values in source-column order with a hexadecimal presence mask; column names are stored once per table. A present null remains distinct from an omitted field stored in the binary or numeric-vector tables. Readers reconstruct the same original dictionaries and also support version-1 JSON-object records. Malformed masks, missing fields and conflicting payloads are rejected. The common quantitative storage version remains 6.

Measured-only queries discard source-null vectors in SQL before expanding cells; non-null vectors still receive per-cell presence and finite-value checks. Missing queries and logical counts retain every null cell. On a 10,000-group spread across the completed native table, the same 30,831 measured records (identical full-field hash) took 30.2 seconds before this filter and 3.4 seconds after it. The query expanded 1,758 non-null vectors instead of 30,000 total vectors. This is a bounded query benchmark, not a full-dataset performance guarantee.

Version 6 declares its projection encoding and completion state explicitly. It does not contain an empty flat measurement view: SQL access to that old internal view fails. Generic dataset creation continues to write version 5, and versions 1–5 remain readable without migration.

The packaged canine importer also requires a final successful build receipt. It pins normalized evidence, compiled lineage, searched FASTA and the existing protein summary; validates the source selection and counts; builds membership and candidate indexes; and projects the native vectors. Common mappings() and relations() queries project the existing indexes into TargetMapping and TargetRelation records without storing another copy. Counts include those logical mappings and relations. Native-table inspection uses the source module's CanineEvidence(dataset.path) adapter. Its summary_group() query connects the baseline summary representative to native records and group links without duplicating the baseline abundance series or asserting unique protein detection.

A bounded comparison of 100 actual native peptide groups (source row IDs 50, 100, …, 5000) reproduced all 13,200 cells from their three 44-channel abundance vectors, field for field. Flat storage occupied 24,891,392 bytes; vector storage occupied 6,557,696 bytes including exact selected source evidence and shared sample/assay metadata. Peak benchmark process RSS was 127,729,664 bytes. This is a storage slice, not a completed canine dataset release or a guarantee of full-dataset size.
